title: Evolution and Ecosystems: Natural Selection, Food Webs, Energy Flow, and Cycles
objectives: You will explain natural selection using its four conditions (variation, inheritance, overproduction, selection) and use population data to describe how a trait becomes more common over generations.
You will identify and evaluate evidence for evolution, including fossils, homologous and vestigial structures, embryos, and DNA and protein comparisons.
You will classify organisms in food chains and food webs as producers, consumers (primary, secondary, tertiary), or decomposers and predict the effects of a change in one population.
You will use the 10% rule to calculate the energy available at each level of an energy pyramid and calculate the actual percentage of energy transferred between levels.
You will describe the main processes of the carbon and nitrogen cycles and interpret data about them.

slides.title: Evolution and Ecosystems
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Explain natural selection with its four conditions
  • Judge evidence for evolution: fossils, body structures, embryos, DNA
  • Classify organisms in food chains and webs and predict changes
  • Use the 10% rule and find real energy-transfer percentages
  • Describe the carbon and nitrogen cycles and read data about them

Plan: Warm-up → 6 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: Last week we looked at how traits pass from parents to children. Today we zoom out: first to whole populations changing over many generations, then to whole ecosystems, where energy and matter move between living things. Life science is about 40 percent of the GED Science test, and these topics show up again and again, almost always with a table, a graph, or a food web to read. You will leave with three tools: a memory sentence for natural selection, a rule for arrows, and a rule for energy.
ask: Have you heard of bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics, or weeds that no longer die from weed killer? (expected answer: any example; we will explain exactly why that happens today)

slides.title: Warm-Up: Genetics Review
slides.board:
1. Write the complementary DNA strand: A T G C C A
  2. Two parents are both Tt. What is the chance a child is tt?
  3. In the genotype Tt (T = tall), is the plant tall or short? Is Tt the genotype or the phenotype?
  4. A sunburn causes a mutation in a skin cell. Can that mutation be passed to the person's children?
steps: 1. A pairs with T, C pairs with G: T A C G G T.
2. Punnett square TT, Tt, Tt, tt: 1 box out of 4 = 1/4 = 25%.
3. Tall, because T is dominant. Tt is the genotype (the letters); tall is the phenotype (the trait you see).
4. No. Only mutations in egg or sperm cells can be inherited. Skin-cell mutations stay with that person.

notes.say: These four questions review last week's genetics, and every one of them matters today. Mutations are where new variation comes from, and only inherited variation can be acted on by natural selection. Give the student about three minutes, then have them tell you each answer before you reveal it.
ask: Why does question 4 matter for evolution? (expected answer: only inherited traits can be passed on and become more common in a population)
notes.answer: 1. T A C G G T. 2. 1/4 or 25%. 3. Tall; Tt is the genotype. 4. No; only mutations in egg or sperm cells (reproductive cells) are inherited.
notes.watch: On question 2, some students answer 50% because half the letters are t. Have them draw the four boxes and count tt boxes only.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: Natural Selection
slides.board:
Evolution = change in the inherited traits of a population over many generations.

Very Interesting Organisms Survive

  • Variation: individuals differ
  • Inheritance: traits pass to offspring through genes
  • Overproduction: more young than can survive, so they compete
  • Selection: better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more

Adaptation = inherited trait that helps survival and reproduction. Fitness = surviving offspring, not strength.

notes.say: Natural selection is the main way populations change, and it needs all four conditions. I want you to write Very Interesting Organisms Survive on your scratch paper. Three ideas the GED tests over and over: populations evolve, not individuals; traits gained during life, like big muscles, are not inherited; and the helpful trait has to exist before the environment changes. The environment does not create the trait. It only picks among traits that are already there.
ask: A weightlifter builds huge muscles. Will his children be born with them? (expected answer: no; it is an acquired trait, not in his genes)
Who is fitter: a big strong deer with one fawn, or a smaller deer with three surviving fawns? (expected answer: the smaller deer; fitness means surviving offspring)
notes.watch: Listen for "the animal adapted because it needed to." Ask: "Did the trait exist before the change? Which individuals had more young?"

slides.title: Worked Example: Beetles and a Pesticide
slides.board:
A farmer sprays a new pesticide every spring. Each fall a scientist tests the beetles.

Year12345
Resistant beetles (%)29316888

Describe the trend and explain it with the four conditions.
steps: Trend: resistance rose every year, from 2% to 88%: an increase of 88 − 2 = 86 percentage points.
Variation: 2% of beetles were already resistant before spraying began.
Inheritance: resistance is genetic, so resistant parents have resistant young.
Overproduction: beetles lay far more eggs than can survive.
Selection: the spray killed most non-resistant beetles, so resistant ones survived and reproduced more. Each generation started with a bigger share of resistant beetles.
Reject: "The beetles became resistant because they were sprayed." The pesticide did not cause resistance; it selected beetles that already had it.

notes.say: Watch how I tie every condition to a fact from the scenario. The trend is the easy part: read the row left to right. The explanation is where the GED catches people, so I finish by naming the wrong idea out loud. The pesticide is the selecting force, not the cause of the trait.
ask: Why did resistance rise faster in the middle years than at the start? (expected answer: there were only a few resistant beetles at first; once more of them were breeding, each generation added many more)

slides.title: We Do: Finch Beaks After a Drought
slides.board:
Seed-eating birds live on an island. During a two-year drought, small soft seeds ran out; mostly large, hard seeds remained. Beak depth is strongly inherited.

Mean beak depth (classroom values): 9.2 mm before the drought, 9.7 mm in the birds that survived.

  1. By how much did mean beak depth change?
  2. Explain the change using the four conditions.
  3. Predict the beak depth of chicks hatched after the drought.
  4. Fix this claim: "Each bird's beak grew deeper from cracking hard seeds."
steps: 1. 9.7 − 9.2 = 0.5 mm deeper.

2. Variation: beaks differed. Inheritance: beak depth is passed on. Overproduction: more birds than the food could support. Selection: deep-beaked birds could crack hard seeds, so more of them survived to breed.
3. Deeper on average than chicks hatched before the drought, because their parents were mostly deep-beaked survivors.
4. Beaks did not grow from use (that would be an acquired change). Birds that already had deeper beaks survived, so the population's average changed.

notes.say: Let's do this one together. You give me each condition and I will write it next to a fact from the story. Notice the question says beak depth is strongly inherited. That sentence is the inheritance condition, handed to you. The GED often gives you the condition in a single sentence of the stimulus.
ask: Which sentence in the story gives you the selection pressure? (expected answer: small soft seeds ran out; only hard seeds remained)
Did any single bird evolve? (expected answer: no; the population's average beak depth changed)
notes.answer: 1. 0.5 mm. 2. Variation, inheritance, overproduction, and selection as shown in the steps. 3. Deeper than before the drought. 4. The claim describes an acquired change in individuals; the correct explanation is that birds that already had deeper beaks survived and reproduced.
notes.watch: Students often answer question 3 with "the same," thinking the drought is over. The chicks inherit their parents' beaks, so the shift carries into the next generation.

slides.title: Big Idea 2: Evidence for Evolution
slides.board:
EvidenceWhat it showsExample
FossilsDeeper layers are older; in-between (transitional) formsEarly whales with small hind legs
Homologous structuresSame bones, different jobs → common ancestorHuman arm, bat wing, whale flipper
Vestigial structuresReduced parts with little or no use nowHuman tailbone, whale hip bones
EmbryosEarly embryos look alikeTails and neck pouches in fish, chick, human
DNA / proteinsFewer differences = more recent common ancestorHuman and chimp proteins nearly identical

Analogous = same job, different build (bird wing, butterfly wing): not evidence of close relationship.

notes.say: Here are five kinds of evidence, and the GED asks you to match an example to its type or to pick the conclusion it supports. The pair people mix up is homologous and analogous. Homologous means same build, possibly different job, and it points to a shared ancestor. Analogous means same job, different build, and it does not. With DNA and protein data, remember: fewer differences means a more recent common ancestor, not that one living species turned into another.
ask: A butterfly wing and a bird wing both fly. Homologous or analogous? (expected answer: analogous; same job, completely different build, so they do not show a close relationship)
What does a vestigial structure suggest about ancestors? (expected answer: the ancestors used that part)
notes.watch: Students may say "humans evolved from chimpanzees." Correct it every time: both came from a common ancestor.

slides.title: Worked Example: Reading Protein Data
slides.board:
Number of amino acid differences between one human protein and the same protein in other animals (classroom values):

AnimalChimpMouseChickenFrogFish
Differences19141924

Which animal shares the most recent common ancestor with humans? Which conclusions are not supported?
steps: Rule: fewer differences = closer relative (more recent common ancestor).
Smallest number: chimpanzee, 1. So humans and chimpanzees share the most recent common ancestor on this list.
Supported: humans are more closely related to mice (9) than to frogs (19).
Not supported: "Humans evolved from chimpanzees." Both descended from an earlier shared ancestor.
Not supported: "Chickens and frogs are close relatives." The table only compares each animal with humans.

notes.say: Data-reading questions about evidence almost always hinge on one rule: fewer differences means a closer relationship. Then the GED tests whether you stay inside the data. This table compares every animal with humans only, so it says nothing about how chickens compare with frogs. That is a favorite trap.
ask: Rank the animals from most to least closely related to humans. (expected answer: chimp, mouse, chicken, frog, fish)

slides.title: We Do: Name That Evidence
slides.board:
Name the type of evidence for each observation.

  1. A cat's front leg and a whale's flipper contain the same set of bones.
  2. Some snakes have tiny leftover hip and leg bones inside their bodies.
  3. A bird's wing and a bat's wing both work for flying, but a butterfly's wing has no bones at all.
  4. Rock layers show a series of horse-like fossils that get larger, with fewer toes, in younger layers.
steps: 1. Homologous structures: same bones, different jobs; suggests a common ancestor.
2. Vestigial structures: reduced parts with no walking use; snake ancestors had legs.
3. The butterfly wing and the bird or bat wing are analogous: same job, built completely differently. They do not show a close relationship.
4. Fossil record: younger layers show changes over time, with in-between forms.

notes.say: Let's sort these together. For each one, you tell me the key word you noticed: same bones, leftover, same job, rock layers. Those clue words point straight to the type of evidence. Number 3 is the tricky one, so take your time on it.
ask: What clue word tells you number 2 is vestigial? (expected answer: tiny leftover bones that are not used for walking)
notes.answer: 1. Homologous structures. 2. Vestigial structures. 3. Analogous structures (butterfly wing versus bird or bat wing); not evidence of close relationship. 4. Fossil record showing change over time.
notes.watch: On number 3, students may call all three wings homologous because they all fly. Ask: "Are they built from the same bones?" A butterfly wing has no bones.

slides.title: Your Turn: Selection and Evidence
slides.board:
1. Mice live in a field. Owls hunt by sight. After a fire, the soil is black. Predict what happens to the share of dark-furred mice over 20 generations, and why.
  2. True or false: "Giraffes got long necks because each giraffe stretched to reach high leaves, and its young were born with longer necks." Explain.
  3. Species X differs from species Y in 6 DNA bases and from species Z in 31 bases. Which species is X more closely related to?
steps: 1. Dark mice will become a larger share. Owls see light mice more easily on black soil, so dark mice survive and reproduce more and pass dark fur on.
2. False. Stretching is an acquired change and is not inherited. Giraffes that already had longer necks reached more food, survived, and had more young.
3. Species Y (6 differences is fewer than 31), so X and Y share a more recent common ancestor.

notes.say: Work these alone; you have four minutes. Tell me your answer and your reason for each, and I will reveal only after you commit. For number 1, I want to hear the words survive, reproduce, and pass on.
notes.answer: 1. The proportion of dark-furred mice increases, because they are harder for owls to see on black soil and so survive and reproduce more. 2. False; acquired traits are not inherited; giraffes with longer necks already present survived and reproduced more. 3. Species Y.
notes.watch: On number 1, a student may say the mice "turn dark to hide." Redirect: individual mice keep their fur color; the share of dark mice changes over generations.

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Food Chains and Food Webs
slides.board:
grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk

RoleGets energy byExample
ProducerPhotosynthesisGrass, algae
Primary consumerEating producersGrasshopper
Secondary consumerEating primary consumersFrog
Tertiary consumerEating secondary consumersSnake
DecomposerBreaking down dead matter and wastesBacteria, fungi

The arrow points toward the eater. Read it as "is eaten by."

notes.say: Every food chain on land starts with the sun and a producer. Count from the producer: one step up is a primary consumer, two steps up is secondary, three is tertiary. The single most important rule today is the arrow. It shows the direction energy moves, so it points to the eater. A food web is many chains linked together, and one animal can sit at different levels in different chains: a mouse eating seeds is a primary consumer, but the same mouse eating a grasshopper is a secondary consumer.
ask: Read this chain out loud using 'is eaten by': grass, grasshopper, frog. (expected answer: grass is eaten by the grasshopper, which is eaten by the frog)
What level is the snake in the chain on the board? (expected answer: tertiary consumer, fourth trophic level)
notes.watch: The classic error is drawing the arrow from hawk to snake because "the hawk attacks the snake." Say every chain aloud with "is eaten by."

slides.title: Worked Example: Remove a Predator
slides.board:
In a coastal kelp forest, sea urchins eat kelp, and sea otters eat sea urchins. Hunters remove most of the sea otters.

Predict the effect on the sea urchins and on the kelp.
steps: Write the chain: kelp → sea urchin → sea otter.
Step 1: fewer otters, so fewer urchins are eaten. Urchins increase.
Step 2: more urchins eat more kelp. Kelp decreases.
Pattern: removing a top predator can cause changes two levels below it. Move one arrow at a time.

notes.say: Whenever a GED question changes one population, I write the chain first, then move one arrow at a time and put an up or down arrow next to each organism. If I try to jump straight to the kelp, I usually get the direction wrong. One step at a time keeps it straight.
ask: What if instead a disease killed most of the kelp? (expected answer: urchins would decrease from lack of food, and then otters would decrease)

slides.title: We Do: Read a Food Web
slides.board:
OrganismEats
Grass(makes its own food)

  1. Name every primary consumer.
  2. Is the mouse a primary or secondary consumer?
  3. Snakes disappear. What happens to the mice first?
steps: 1. Rabbit, grasshopper, and mouse (when it eats seeds) all eat a producer.
2. Both. Eating seeds: primary. Eating grasshoppers: secondary.
3. Fewer snakes eat mice, so mice increase. (Then hawks may eat more mice, and grasshoppers may decrease.)

notes.say: A food web on the GED is often given as a table like this one. I read each row as 'this animal eats that.' Let's work through the three questions together. On number 2, the answer depends on which food chain you follow, and the GED likes that idea.
ask: Which organism is at the top of every chain it belongs to? (expected answer: the hawk)
notes.answer: 1. Rabbit, grasshopper, mouse. 2. Both: primary when it eats grass seeds, secondary when it eats grasshoppers. 3. The mouse population increases.
notes.watch: Some students leave the mouse out of number 1 because it also eats grasshoppers. Point back to the seeds.

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Energy Pyramids and the 10% Rule
slides.board:
Only about 10% of the energy at one level is stored in the next level. The other 90% is used for life processes such as moving and keeping warm (and leaves as heat), or is in parts that are never eaten or digested.

LevelEnergy (kcal)
Tertiary consumers10
Secondary consumers100
Primary consumers1,000
Producers10,000

Up one level: × 0.10. Down one level: × 10.
Energy flows one way; matter cycles.

notes.say: Each step in a food chain is a trophic level. An energy pyramid is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top because each level keeps only about a tenth of the energy below it. That is why there are far fewer hawks than mice, and why food chains rarely go past four or five levels. The math is simple: going up, multiply by 0.10, which just moves the decimal point one place left. Going down, multiply by 10.
ask: Why can't an ecosystem support as many hawks as mice? (expected answer: each level has only about 10% of the energy of the level below)
Does energy get recycled back to the producers? (expected answer: no; it leaves as heat; matter is recycled, energy is not)
notes.watch: Students subtract 10% instead of keeping 10% (10,000 − 1,000 = 9,000). Sanity check: each level should be one tenth of the one below, not nine tenths.

slides.title: Worked Example: Forward and Backward
slides.board:
Grassland producers capture 50,000 kcal. Chain: grass → mouse → snake → hawk.

  1. How much energy reaches the hawks?
  2. What percent of the producers' energy is that?
  3. A different hawk population needs 30 kcal. How much must its producers capture?
steps: 1. Mice: 50,000 × 0.10 = 5,000. Snakes: 5,000 × 0.10 = 500. Hawks: 500 × 0.10 = 50 kcal.
2. 50 ÷ 50,000 = 0.001 = 0.1% (three steps: 0.10 × 0.10 × 0.10).
3. Backward, × 10 each step: snakes 30 × 10 = 300; mice 300 × 10 = 3,000; producers 3,000 × 10 = 30,000 kcal.
Check: count the arrows, not the organisms. Grass to hawk is 3 arrows, so 3 steps.

notes.say: I write one line per level so I never lose count. The key is counting arrows, not organisms: four organisms means three arrows, which means three multiplications. Going backward is the same rule in reverse, times ten for each arrow.
ask: How many times did we multiply by 0.10 to get from grass to hawk, and why not four? (expected answer: three times; there are three arrows between four organisms)
notes.watch: The extra-step error: multiplying four times for four organisms gives 5 kcal. Point to the arrows and count them.

slides.title: Worked Example: The Real Percentage
slides.board:
A lake study (classroom values, kcal per square meter per year):

LevelEnergy
Algae (producers)15,000
Zooplankton (primary)1,200
Small fish (secondary)150

What percent of the zooplankton's energy reached the small fish?
steps: Formula: (higher level ÷ level below) × 100.
0.125 × 100 = 12.5%, a bit more than the 10% rule predicts.
Compare: algae to zooplankton is 1,200 ÷ 15,000 = 0.08 = 8%. Real ecosystems are near 10%, not exactly 10%.

notes.say: The 10% rule is an estimate. When the GED gives measured data, it may ask for the actual percentage. Put the higher level on top, because you are asking what fraction of the lower level's energy made it up. The calculator is available on the science test, so use it.
ask: What would you get if you divided the wrong way, 1,200 by 150? (expected answer: 8, which is a ratio, not a percent; the percentage must be less than 100)
notes.watch: Students divide the bigger number by the smaller one. Remind them: a transfer percentage is always well under 100%.

slides.title: We Do: Pond Pyramid
slides.board:
Pond producers capture 8,000 kcal.
Chain: algae → snail → crayfish → raccoon

  1. How much energy reaches the crayfish?
  2. Which organism is the tertiary consumer, and at which trophic level?
  3. Measured data show the snails really held 720 kcal. What percent of the algae's energy is that?
steps: 1. Snail: 8,000 × 0.10 = 800. Crayfish: 800 × 0.10 = 80 kcal.
2. The raccoon: algae is level 1, snail 2, crayfish 3, raccoon 4.
3. 720 ÷ 8,000 = 0.09 = 9%.

notes.say: You call out each line and I will write it. Say the multiplication before the answer, so I can hear your method. Notice that trophic levels are counted from the producer as level 1, which is why the tertiary consumer sits at level 4.
ask: What is the first line for number 1? (expected answer: 8,000 times 0.10 equals 800 for the snails)
notes.watch: On number 2, students often say "level 3" because it is the third consumer. Trophic levels count the producer as level 1.

slides.title: Your Turn: Webs and Energy
slides.board:
1. Chain: phytoplankton → krill → penguin → leopard seal. Phytoplankton capture 60,000 kcal. How much reaches the leopard seals?
  2. An owl population (secondary consumers) needs 40 kcal. How much must the producers capture?
  3. A study measured 2,500 kcal in caterpillars and 200 kcal in the birds that eat them. What percent was transferred?
  4. In the chain on line 1, a disease kills most krill. What happens to the penguins? To the phytoplankton?
steps: 1. 60,000 → 6,000 → 600 → 60 kcal.
2. Two arrows down: 40 × 10 = 400; 400 × 10 = 4,000 kcal.
3. 200 ÷ 2,500 = 0.08 = 8%.
4. Penguins decrease (less food). Phytoplankton increase (fewer krill eating them).

notes.say: Four problems, five minutes. Write every line of the math on your paper. When you are ready, read me your answers and your first line of work for each calculation.
notes.answer: 1. 60 kcal. 2. 4,000 kcal. 3. 8%. 4. Penguins decrease; phytoplankton increase.
notes.watch: On number 2, watch for 40,000 (an extra step). A secondary consumer is two arrows above the producers.

slides.title: Big Idea 5: The Carbon Cycle
slides.board:
Removes CO2 from the air

  • Photosynthesis (plants, algae)
  • Ocean water absorbing CO2

Adds CO2 to the air

  • Cellular respiration (all living things)
  • Decomposition
  • Burning fuels, including fossil fuels
  • Volcanic eruptions

Stores: living things, soil, oceans, limestone rock, fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas made from ancient organisms).

notes.say: Energy flows one way, but matter cycles, and carbon is the main example. Only two processes on our list take carbon dioxide out of the air: photosynthesis and the ocean absorbing it. Everything else on the right puts it back. Plants do both photosynthesis and respiration, all the time they are alive. Burning fossil fuels matters because it releases, in a few years, carbon that was locked away for millions of years.
ask: Name the one living process that removes CO<sub>2</sub> from the air. (expected answer: photosynthesis)
Do plants carry out cellular respiration? (expected answer: yes, day and night)
notes.watch: Students mix up photosynthesis and respiration. Anchor it: photosynthesis builds sugar from CO2, so it takes CO2 in; respiration breaks sugar down, so it gives CO2 off.

slides.title: Big Idea 6: The Nitrogen Cycle
slides.board:
Air is about 78% nitrogen gas (N2), but plants and animals cannot use it directly. Bacteria do most of the work.

  1. Fixation: N2 → ammonia (bacteria in soil and in root nodules of beans, peas, clover); lightning also fixes a little N2
  2. Nitrification: ammonia → nitrates (soil bacteria)
  3. Assimilation: plants absorb nitrates and build proteins and DNA; animals eat plants
  4. Ammonification: decomposers return ammonia from dead matter and wastes
  5. Denitrification: nitrates → N2 back to the air (bacteria)

notes.say: Living things need nitrogen to build proteins and DNA, and the air is full of it, but almost nothing can use nitrogen gas directly. Bacteria are the heroes of this cycle: they fix it, they convert it to nitrates, and they return it to the air. On the GED you will most often be asked which step is which, and which organisms do the work. If you remember that fixation brings nitrogen in and denitrification sends it back out, you have the two ends of the cycle.
ask: Which step turns nitrogen gas into a form plants can use? (expected answer: nitrogen fixation)
Which step sends nitrogen back to the air? (expected answer: denitrification)
notes.watch: Students think plants take nitrogen gas straight from the air through their leaves. They cannot; plants take in nitrates and ammonia through their roots.

slides.title: Worked Example: Seasonal CO<sub>2</sub> Data
slides.board:
A Northern Hemisphere station measures CO2 (ppm) in the air. (Simplified values; the real Mauna Loa, Hawaii, record shows the same pattern: a peak around May, a low around September, a swing of about 6 ppm.)

MonthJanMaySepDec
CO2420.8424.0418.0420.9

How much does CO2 fall from May to September? Explain the drop and the rise afterward.
steps: Change: 424.0 − 418.0 = 6.0 ppm drop.
May to September is the growing season. Leafy plants do a lot of photosynthesis, removing CO2 faster than respiration and decomposition add it.
After September, leaves fall and photosynthesis slows, but respiration and decomposition of fallen leaves continue, so CO2 rises again.
Reject: "burning fuel removes CO<sub>2</sub>" and "animals stop respiring in summer." Burning adds CO<sub>2</sub>, and respiration never stops.

notes.say: This is how the carbon cycle shows up on the GED: as data. First I compute the change, then I match the direction to a process. A fall in CO<sub>2</sub> needs a process that removes it, and there are only two on our list. In a summer pattern, it is photosynthesis.
ask: Why would the swing be smaller in the Southern Hemisphere? (expected answer: it has much less land covered with leafy plants, so seasonal photosynthesis changes less)

slides.title: Worked Example: Beans Before Corn
slides.board:
A farmer plants soybeans one year and corn the next. Without extra fertilizer, corn planted after soybeans grows better than corn planted after corn.

Explain using the nitrogen cycle.
steps: Corn needs nitrogen to build proteins, and it takes nitrogen in as nitrates or ammonia through its roots.
Soybeans are legumes. Bacteria in their root nodules fix nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia.
When soybean roots and leftover plants decay, decomposers release that nitrogen into the soil, and other bacteria turn it into nitrates.
So the soil holds more usable nitrogen for the corn. Reject: "soybean leaves absorb nitrogen gas from the air." The bacteria do the fixing.

notes.say: This is called crop rotation, and it is a real farming practice that the GED likes because it connects the cycle to everyday life. Walk through it as a chain of steps: fixation in the nodules, decay, nitrification, and finally the corn absorbing nitrates. Each step names who does the work.
ask: What organisms make this work? (expected answer: nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soybean root nodules)

slides.title: Your Turn: Cycles
slides.board:
1. Sort: photosynthesis, burning gasoline, respiration, ocean absorbing CO2, volcano erupting. Which remove CO2 from the air?
  2. Name the nitrogen-cycle step: soil bacteria change ammonia into nitrates.
  3. A forest is cut down and burned. Give two reasons atmospheric CO2 goes up.
steps: 1. Remove: photosynthesis and ocean absorbing CO2. (Burning, respiration, and volcanoes add it.)
2. Nitrification.
3. (a) Burning releases the carbon stored in the wood as CO<sub>2</sub>. (b) With the trees gone, less CO<sub>2</sub> is removed by photosynthesis.

notes.say: Three minutes for these. On number 3, I am listening for one reason about adding CO<sub>2</sub> and one about removing less, because that two-sided answer is what a GED question will reward.
notes.answer: 1. Photosynthesis and the ocean absorbing CO2. 2. Nitrification. 3. Burning adds the wood's stored carbon to the air as CO2, and fewer trees remain to remove CO2 by photosynthesis.
notes.watch: On number 2, students say "fixation." Ask: "Is the nitrogen starting as a gas from the air?" It starts as ammonia, so it is nitrification.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Explain the Change
slides.board:
A rocky shore has thin-shelled and thick-shelled snails; shell thickness is inherited. In 2008, crabs that crush thin shells arrived. From 2008 to 2018, thick-shelled snails rose from 20% to 80% of the population.

Which statement best explains this change?

A. Snails grew thicker shells during their lives to protect themselves from the new crabs.
B. The crabs caused mutations that turned thin-shelled snails into thick-shelled ones.
C. Thick-shelled snails survived crab attacks more often and passed thick shells to their young.
D. The total number of snails increased, so there was more food for thick-shelled snails.
steps: A is out. It describes individuals changing during their lives, an acquired change. Populations evolve; individuals do not.
B is out. Mutations are random. The crabs did not create the trait; thick-shelled snails existed before 2008 (20%).
D is out. Nothing says the population grew, and more food would not explain why one shell type increased.
C is correct. Variation already existed, shell thickness is inherited, and crabs selected against thin shells. Survivors passed thick shells on, so their share rose.

notes.say: This is the most common natural-selection question on the GED: which statement best explains the change. Wrong answers are built from the three traps we named: individuals changing, the environment creating the trait, and an explanation that does not connect to survival. Eliminate them one at a time and say why out loud.
ask: Which number in the stem proves the trait existed before the crabs came? (expected answer: 20% thick-shelled snails in 2008)
notes.answer: C. Thick-shelled snails survived crab attacks more often and passed thick shells to their offspring. A describes an acquired change, B claims the environment created the trait, and D is unsupported and does not explain why one shell type increased.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Energy at the Top
slides.board:
In a meadow, producers capture 24,000 kcal per square meter per year. Food chain: clover → rabbit → fox → eagle.

Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the eagles?

A. 2.4 kcal
B. 24 kcal
C. 240 kcal
D. 17,496 kcal
steps: Count the arrows: clover → rabbit → fox → eagle = 3 arrows.
C is out. 240 kcal is the fox level: 24,000 → 2,400 → 240. That stops one step short.
A is out. 2.4 kcal takes four steps, one for each organism instead of each arrow.
D is out. 17,496 comes from subtracting 10% three times (24,000 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9). The rule says 10% is passed on, not lost.
B is correct. 24,000 × 0.10 = 2,400; × 0.10 = 240; × 0.10 = 24 kcal.

notes.say: Every wrong choice here comes from a real error: stopping a step early, taking an extra step, or subtracting instead of keeping 10%. When the answers are all numbers, I solve it first on paper and then look for my number, and I check that my answer is about a thousandth of the starting energy for three steps.
ask: How could you check B quickly? (expected answer: three steps means divide by 1,000; 24,000 divided by 1,000 is 24)
notes.answer: B. 24 kcal. Three arrows: 24,000 → 2,400 → 240 → 24. C stops one step early, A takes an extra step, and D subtracts 10% at each step.

slides.title: Test Strategy: Check the Direction First
slides.board:
Before you read the answer choices, jot one arrow on your scratch paper:

  • Population table: is the trait going ↑ or ↓?
  • Food web: which way is energy moving? (toward the eater)
  • Cycle: is the process adding or removing?
  • Energy math: going up = × 0.10; going down = × 10

Many wrong choices simply reverse the direction. Ten seconds catches them. Use the on-screen calculator for every percentage.

notes.say: This is the habit to carry into the test. On this topic, the GED builds wrong answers by flipping directions: the arrow points the wrong way, the trait goes the wrong way, or a process that adds carbon dioxide is described as removing it. Spend ten seconds writing your arrow before you look at the choices, and you will cross out half of them immediately. And for any energy or percentage question, use the calculator; there is no prize for mental math.
ask: For the question 'Which process would lower CO<sub>2</sub> in the air?', what arrow do you write first? (expected answer: down, so I need a process that removes CO<sub>2</sub>: photosynthesis or ocean absorption)

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
1. Natural selection: Variation, Inheritance, Overproduction, Selection. Populations evolve; acquired traits are not inherited.
  2. Evidence: fossils, homologous and vestigial structures, embryos, DNA. Fewer differences = more recent common ancestor.
  3. Arrows point to the eater. Remove a predator: prey ↑, prey's food ↓.
  4. About 10% passes up each level. Actual % = higher ÷ lower × 100.
  5. Energy flows; matter cycles. Photosynthesis removes CO2; bacteria fix nitrogen and return it to the air.

Then do Practice Set A; if you score under 80 percent, take Set B. Finish with the Exit Check, where you need 6 of 8.
ask: What are the four conditions of natural selection? (expected answer: variation, inheritance, overproduction, selection)
Producers have 6,000 kcal. How much reaches the secondary consumers? (expected answer: 60 kcal)
Does energy cycle? (expected answer: no; energy flows one way and leaves as heat; matter cycles)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
This lesson connects two big ideas. First, how populations of living things change over many generations (evolution). Second, how living things are linked by food, energy, and the cycling of matter (ecosystems). On the GED, these topics almost always come with a table, graph, or food web, so you will practice reading data as you learn. You will learn to:

  • Explain natural selection with its four conditions.
  • Recognize the evidence for evolution: fossils, body structures, embryos, and DNA.
  • Classify organisms in food chains and webs and predict what happens when one population changes.
  • Use the 10% rule and calculate real energy-transfer percentages.
  • Describe the carbon and nitrogen cycles and read data about them.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Use the hint if you get stuck.

screens.title: Evolution and the four conditions
screens.html:
Evolution is a change in the inherited traits of a population over many generations. The main way it happens is natural selection, which needs four conditions. Remember them with Very Interesting Organisms Survive:

ConditionWhat it means
VariationIndividuals in a population have different traits.
InheritanceTraits pass from parents to offspring through genes.
OverproductionMore offspring are born than can survive, so they compete.
SelectionIndividuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common.

An adaptation is an inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment, such as fur that matches the snow.

example.prompt: A patient takes an antibiotic. Most of the infecting bacteria die, but a few carry a gene that makes them resistant. Match each fact to a condition.
steps: Variation: a few bacteria were already resistant; most were not.
Inheritance: resistant bacteria pass the gene to the cells they divide into.
Overproduction: bacteria multiply very quickly, far beyond what can survive.
Selection: the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria, so resistant ones become a larger share.
example.answer: All four conditions are present, so the population becomes more resistant. The antibiotic did not cause resistance; it selected it.

check.prompt: A female sea turtle lays about 100 eggs, but only one or two of the young usually live long enough to breed. Which condition of natural selection does this describe?
options: Overproduction
Variation
Inheritance
Selection
why: Variation is about differences among individuals, such as shell color or size. This fact is about how many young are produced compared with how many survive.
Inheritance is about traits passing from parent to offspring. Nothing here says which traits the young received.
Selection is about which individuals survive because of their traits. This fact only says most young die; it does not say why some survive.
check.hint: Look at the numbers: how many are born compared with how many survive?
check.explain: Producing about 100 eggs when only one or two survive to breed is overproduction: more offspring than the environment can support, so they compete. Selection is the tempting answer, but selection would need a trait that helps some turtles survive more than others, and this fact names no trait.

screens.title: Natural selection in the data
screens.html:
On the GED, natural selection usually comes as a table or graph of a population over time. Use this routine:

  1. Read the trend. Which group goes up, and which goes down?
  2. Find the percent if asked: part ÷ total × 100. Always divide by the total for that year.
  3. Explain with the four conditions. Name the selecting force (a predator, a drought, a poison) and say who survived and reproduced more.

Remember that the trait goes up as a share of the population. The total population can stay steady while one type becomes more common.

example.prompt: A beetle population was tested each fall after spraying. Year 1: 6 of 300 beetles were resistant. Year 5: 264 of 300 were resistant. Describe the change as percents.
steps: Change: 88 − 2 = 86 percentage points. The spray selected resistant beetles, which survived and reproduced more.
example.answer: Resistant beetles rose from 2% to 88% of the population.

check.prompt: A cricket population of 400 is tested, and 96 crickets are resistant to an insecticide. What percent of the population is resistant? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: You divided 96 by the 304 crickets that are not resistant. A percent of the population divides by the whole population: 96 ÷ 400.
0.24 is the decimal. Multiply by 100 to write it as a percent: 24.
You divided the total by the part (400 ÷ 96). Put the part on top: 96 ÷ 400 = 0.24.

check.explain:
96 ÷ 400 = 0.24

0.24 × 100 = 24%

Dividing by the non-resistant crickets (96 ÷ 304 ≈ 31.6%) is the most common slip. The denominator is always the whole population.

screens.title: Three traps about evolution
screens.html:
The GED tests these three ideas again and again:

  1. Populations evolve; individuals do not. One lizard cannot change its genes during its life. The percentage of lizards with a trait changes from one generation to the next.
  2. Acquired traits are not inherited. Big muscles from lifting weights or a scar are not passed to children.
  3. Variation comes first. Mutations are random. The environment does not create a helpful trait because an animal "needs" it. It only selects among traits that already exist.

Also: fitness in biology means reproductive success, not strength. The fittest individual is the one that leaves the most surviving offspring.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how giraffes came to have long necks?
options: Giraffes with longer necks reached more food, survived and bred more, and passed long necks to their young.
Each giraffe stretched its neck to reach high leaves, and its young were then born with longer necks.
A shortage of low leaves caused mutations that gave every giraffe in the herd a longer neck.
The strongest giraffes fought off the others, so strength, not neck length, became more common.
why: Stretching during life is an acquired change. It does not change the genes in eggs or sperm, so it cannot be inherited.
The environment does not create mutations on demand. Longer necks had to exist in some giraffes before the leaf shortage could favor them.
Fitness means leaving surviving offspring, not winning fights, and this statement does not explain how long necks became common.
check.hint: Which choice has an existing trait, survival, reproduction, and inheritance?
check.explain: Natural selection works on traits that already vary: giraffes with longer necks reached more food, survived and reproduced more, and passed the trait on. The stretching explanation is the classic wrong idea; an acquired change is not inherited. The mutation choice wrongly says the environment caused the trait.

screens.title: Evidence from body structures and fossils
screens.html:
• Fossil record: deeper rock layers are older. Fossils show how living things changed over time, including transitional (in-between) forms, such as early whales that still had small hind legs.
  • Homologous structures: the same basic bones used for different jobs: a human arm, a bat wing, a whale flipper, a cat's front leg. Same structure suggests a common ancestor.
  • Vestigial structures: reduced parts with little or no use now, such as the human tailbone or tiny hip bones inside some whales. They suggest the ancestors used those parts.

Analogous structures do the same job but are built differently, such as a bird wing and a butterfly wing. They do not show a close relationship. Look for the same build, not the same job.

check.prompt: Drag each observation to the type of structure it describes.
choices: A human arm and a whale flipper contain the same set of bones.
A cat's front leg and a bat's wing have matching bones in the same order.
A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing are both used for flying.
A shark's fin and a dolphin's flipper both steer in water, but only the flipper has finger bones.
Some whales have tiny hip bones that are not attached to any legs.
Blind cave fish have small eyes covered by skin.
check.why: The most common mistake is calling the bird wing and butterfly wing homologous because both fly. Homologous means the same bones; a butterfly wing has no bones at all, so the pair is analogous.
check.hint: Same bones = homologous. Same job, different build = analogous. Leftover part with little use = vestigial.
check.explain:
• Homologous: human arm and whale flipper; cat leg and bat wing. Same bones, different jobs.
  • Analogous: bird wing and butterfly wing; shark fin and dolphin flipper. Same job, different structure.
  • Vestigial: whale hip bones; skin-covered cave fish eyes. Reduced parts that no longer do their original job.

Sorting by job instead of by structure is the usual error.

screens.title: Evidence from embryos and DNA
screens.html:
Embryos: early embryos of fish, chickens, and humans look alike. All have a tail and a series of pouches in the neck region. This suggests they share a common ancestor.

DNA and proteins: scientists compare the DNA bases in a gene, or the amino acids in a protein, between species. The rule:

Fewer differences = closer relationship = more recent common ancestor.

Stay inside the data. Few differences between humans and chimpanzees means a recent common ancestor; it does not mean humans came from today's chimpanzees. And if a table compares every species only with humans, it tells you nothing about how two of the other species compare with each other.

check.prompt: Scientists counted differences in a gene between a gray wolf and three other animals: coyote, 4 differences; red fox, 21; house cat, 52. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Gray wolves share a more recent common ancestor with coyotes than with red foxes.
Gray wolves are most closely related to house cats, which had the largest count.
Gray wolves evolved directly from coyotes, because only 4 bases are different.
Red foxes and house cats are more closely related to each other than either is to gray wolves.
why: You reversed the rule. More differences means a more distant relationship, so house cats (52) are the least closely related on the list.
Few differences show a recent common ancestor, not that one living species turned into another. Wolves and coyotes both descend from an earlier species.
The data compare each animal only with the gray wolf. They give no information about foxes compared with cats.
check.hint: Fewer differences means a closer relationship.
check.explain: Coyotes have 4 differences and red foxes have 21. Since 4 < 21, wolves are more closely related to coyotes, so wolves and coyotes share a more recent common ancestor. The "evolved directly from coyotes" choice is tempting, but small differences point to a shared ancestor, not to one living species becoming another.

screens.title: Producers, consumers, and decomposers
screens.html:
Every ecosystem needs energy, and on land almost all of it starts with the sun.

  • Producers (plants, algae) make their own food by photosynthesis.
  • Primary consumers eat producers. Secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
  • Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead organisms and wastes from every level and return nutrients to the soil.

Each step is a trophic level, counted from the producers as level 1. So a primary consumer is level 2, a secondary consumer is level 3, and a tertiary consumer is level 4.

example.prompt: Label each organism: oak leaves → caterpillar → warbler → hawk.
steps: Oak leaves make food by photosynthesis: producer (level 1).
Caterpillar eats the producer: primary consumer (level 2). Warbler eats the caterpillar: secondary consumer (level 3).
Hawk eats the warbler: tertiary consumer (level 4).

check.prompt:
Food chain on a rocky shore: seaweed → periwinkle snail → crab → gull.

The crab is a {{0}}. The seaweed is a {{1}}. Bacteria that break down a dead gull are {{2}}.

options: primary consumer
secondary consumer
tertiary consumer
producer
why: The snail is the primary consumer because it eats the seaweed. The crab eats the snail, one level higher.
The gull is the tertiary consumer. Count again: seaweed, snail, crab is the third organism, so the crab is the second consumer.
Producers make their own food. The crab eats snails, so it is a consumer.

options: producer
primary consumer
decomposer
why: Seaweed eats nothing. It makes food by photosynthesis, so it is the producer.
Decomposers break down dead matter. Seaweed is a living producer at the start of the chain.

options: producers
decomposers
tertiary consumers
why: Producers make their own food from sunlight. Bacteria breaking down a dead body are getting energy from dead matter.
Tertiary consumers eat living secondary consumers. Organisms that break down dead remains are decomposers.

check.hint: Start counting at the seaweed. The first eater is the primary consumer.
check.explain:
Seaweed makes its own food, so it is the producer. The snail eats seaweed (primary consumer), and the crab eats the snail, so the crab is the secondary consumer. Bacteria that break down dead organisms are decomposers.

The most common slip is calling the crab a tertiary consumer because it is the third organism. Count consumers only: snail first, crab second.

screens.title: Reading food chains and webs
screens.html:
In a food chain, the arrow points toward the eater. It shows the direction energy moves. Read each arrow as "is eaten by":

grass → grasshopper → frog = grass is eaten by the grasshopper, which is eaten by the frog.

A food web is many food chains linked together. One organism can sit at different levels in different chains. A mouse that eats seeds is a primary consumer; the same mouse eating a grasshopper is a secondary consumer.

On the GED, a food web is often given as a table of "what each organism eats." Turn each row into arrows pointing from the food to the eater.

check.prompt: Rabbits eat clover, and foxes eat rabbits. Which food chain is drawn correctly?
options: clover → rabbit → fox
fox → rabbit → clover
rabbit → clover → fox
clover → fox → rabbit
why: These arrows point from the eater to the food, which reverses the flow of energy. The arrow should point toward the eater.
Rabbits do not get eaten by clover. Start the chain with the producer, clover, then the animal that eats it.
Foxes do not eat clover. The fox eats the rabbit, so the rabbit must come right before the fox.
check.hint: Start with the producer. Read each arrow as "is eaten by."
check.explain: Clover is the producer, the rabbit eats clover, and the fox eats the rabbit. Energy moves clover → rabbit → fox, so the arrows point toward each eater. The reversed chain (fox → rabbit → clover) is the most common error: it follows who attacks whom instead of where the energy goes.

screens.title: Predicting changes in a food web
screens.html:
When one population changes, effects ripple through the web. Use this routine:

  1. Write the chain that includes the changed organism.
  2. Move one arrow at a time. Put ↑ or ↓ next to each organism.
  3. Fewer predators → prey ↑. More prey → the prey's food ↓. Less food → the eaters ↓.

Removing a top predator often affects organisms two levels below it.

example.prompt: In a kelp forest, sea urchins eat kelp, and sea otters eat sea urchins. Hunters remove most of the otters. Predict the effects.
steps: Chain: kelp → sea urchin → sea otter.
Otters ↓, so fewer urchins are eaten: urchins ↑.
Urchins ↑, so more kelp is eaten: kelp ↓.

check.prompt: In a lake, the food chain is algae → zooplankton → minnows → bass. Fishing removes most of the bass. Which pair of effects is most likely?
options: Minnows increase, and then zooplankton decrease.
Minnows decrease, and then zooplankton increase.
Minnows increase, and then algae decrease right away.
Zooplankton increase, because bass no longer eat them.
why: You reversed the first step. With fewer bass eating them, minnows survive in larger numbers, so they increase.
Minnows do not eat algae. More minnows eat more zooplankton; the algae are one more step away and would likely increase as zooplankton decrease.
Bass do not eat zooplankton in this chain; they eat minnows. Follow the arrows one level at a time.
check.hint: Start at the bass and move down one arrow at a time.
check.explain: Bass ↓ means fewer minnows are eaten, so minnows increase. More minnows eat more zooplankton, so zooplankton decrease. (With fewer zooplankton grazing, algae would then likely increase.) The tempting choice that says minnows decrease reverses the direction of the first step.

screens.title: The 10% rule
screens.html:
Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is stored in the bodies of the next level. The other 90% is used for life processes such as moving, breathing, and staying warm, and ends up as heat, or is in parts that are never eaten or digested. That is why an energy pyramid is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top.

Going up one level: multiply by 0.10 (move the decimal point one place left).
Count the arrows, not the organisms. Four organisms in a chain = three arrows = three steps.

Do not subtract 10%. Only 10% is kept at each step.

example.prompt: Producers in a forest capture 20,000 kcal. How much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
steps: Producers to primary consumers: 20,000 × 0.10 = 2,000 kcal.
Primary to secondary consumers: 2,000 × 0.10 = 200 kcal.
Check: two arrows, two steps. Not 20,000 − 2,000 = 18,000; that subtracts instead of keeping 10%.

check.prompt: The producers in a prairie capture 70,000 kcal per square meter per year. Using the 10% rule, how much energy is available to the secondary consumers? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 7,000 kcal is the primary consumer level. Secondary consumers are one more step up: 7,000 × 0.10 = 700.
You subtracted 10% at each step (70,000 × 0.9 × 0.9). The rule says only about 10% is passed on, so multiply by 0.10.
70 kcal takes three steps, which would be the tertiary consumers. Producers to secondary consumers is two arrows.

check.hint: Two steps up: producers to primary, then primary to secondary. Multiply by 0.10 each time.
check.explain:
Primary consumers: 70,000 × 0.10 = 7,000 kcal

Secondary consumers: 7,000 × 0.10 = 700 kcal

Stopping after one step (7,000) and subtracting 10% each time (56,700) are the two most common errors.

screens.title: Working backward
screens.html:
Sometimes the GED gives you the energy a top consumer needs and asks how much the producers must capture. Go down the pyramid: multiply by 10 for each arrow.

Up one level: × 0.10. Down one level: × 10.

Sanity check: the producers always have far more energy than any consumer. If your producer number is smaller than the consumer number, you went the wrong way.

example.prompt: A hawk population (tertiary consumers) in the chain grass → mouse → snake → hawk needs 30 kcal. How much must the grass capture?
steps: Snakes: 30 × 10 = 300 kcal.
Mice: 300 × 10 = 3,000 kcal.
Grass: 3,000 × 10 = 30,000 kcal.

check.prompt: In the chain algae → insect larvae → trout, the trout (secondary consumers) need 25 kcal per square meter per year. Using the 10% rule, how much energy must the algae capture? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 250 kcal is the insect larvae level. Go down one more arrow to the algae: 250 × 10 = 2,500.
You multiplied by 0.10, which moves up the pyramid. Going down to the producers, multiply by 10 for each arrow.
That is three steps, but algae to trout is only two arrows. 25 × 10 × 10 = 2,500.

check.hint: Going down the pyramid, multiply by 10 for each arrow.
check.explain:
Insect larvae: 25 × 10 = 250 kcal

Algae: 250 × 10 = 2,500 kcal

Two arrows means two multiplications by 10. Multiplying by 0.10 (2.5 or 0.25) goes the wrong direction; the producers must have more energy than the trout.

screens.title: The real transfer percentage
screens.html:
The 10% rule is an estimate. Real measurements are usually somewhere around 5% to 20%. When the GED gives you measured data, it may ask for the actual percentage:

Actual % = (energy in the higher level ÷ energy in the level below) × 100

Two checks: the higher level goes on top, and the answer must be well under 100%. Also notice the difference between the greatest amount of energy moved and the greatest percentage. The bottom step always moves the most kilocalories, but not always the highest percent.

example.prompt: A study measured 900 kcal in a level of primary consumers and 72 kcal in the secondary consumers that eat them. What percentage was passed on?
steps: Higher level on top: 72 ÷ 900 = 0.08.
Compare with the rule: 8% is a little less than 10%.

check.prompt: Scientists measured 2,400 kcal in a population of grasshoppers and 180 kcal in the frogs that eat them. What percent of the grasshoppers' energy was transferred to the frogs? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: You divided 2,400 by 180. Put the higher level (frogs) on top: 180 ÷ 2,400 = 0.075.
92.5% is the share that was not passed on. The question asks for the share transferred: 180 ÷ 2,400 × 100.
0.075 is the decimal. Multiply by 100 to get the percent: 7.5.

check.hint: Divide the frogs' energy by the grasshoppers' energy, then multiply by 100.
check.explain:
180 ÷ 2,400 = 0.075

0.075 × 100 = 7.5%

This is a little less than the 10% rule predicts. Dividing the other way gives 13.3, a ratio rather than a percent; a transfer percentage is always far below 100.

screens.title: Energy flows; matter cycles
screens.html:
Energy enters an ecosystem as sunlight and moves one way: sun → producers → consumers → heat. At every level, most of it leaves as heat that living things cannot use again. Energy is not destroyed; it changes form, but heat cannot be captured to power another food chain. So ecosystems need a constant supply of sunlight.

Matter is different. The carbon, nitrogen, and water atoms in living things are used again and again. Decomposers break down dead matter and return the atoms to the soil, water, and air, where producers can take them up again.

Energy flows. Matter cycles.

check.prompt: Why is less energy available at each higher trophic level? Select two answers.
options: Organisms use most of the energy they take in to move, breathe, and keep warm, and it leaves as heat.
Some parts of the organisms below, such as bones, roots, or fur, are never eaten or digested.
Decomposers return energy to the producers, so less is left for the consumers.
Animals at higher levels are larger, so they need less energy per kilogram.
Energy is destroyed each time one organism eats another.
why: Decomposers recycle matter, not energy. The energy they use also leaves as heat; it does not go back to the producers.
Body size does not explain the pattern, and this statement says nothing about energy being lost between levels.
Energy is never destroyed. It is converted, mostly to heat, which living things cannot use for food.
check.hint: Where does the 90% go? Think about what living things do with energy and what does not get eaten.
check.explain:
Most of the energy an organism takes in is used for life processes and released as heat, and some of the lower level is never eaten or digested. Both mean only about 10% ends up stored in the next level.

"Energy is destroyed" is tempting but wrong: energy changes form (to heat); it is not destroyed. Decomposers recycle matter, not energy.

screens.title: The carbon cycle
screens.html:
Carbon moves between the air, living things, oceans, soil, and rocks.

Removes CO2 from the airAdds CO2 to the air
Photosynthesis by plants and algaeCellular respiration by all living things
Ocean water absorbing CO2Decomposition of dead matter
Burning fuels, including fossil fuels
Volcanic eruptions

Carbon is stored in living things, soil, ocean water, rocks such as limestone, and fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas), which formed from organisms that lived millions of years ago. Remember that plants carry out both photosynthesis and cellular respiration.

check.prompt: Drag each process to show whether it adds CO2 to the air or removes CO2 from the air.
choices: Photosynthesis by a forest
Cellular respiration by deer
Burning gasoline in a car
Ocean water absorbing CO<sub>2</sub>
Fungi decomposing a fallen log
A volcano erupting
check.why: The most common mistake is putting decomposition under "removes" because it gets rid of dead matter. Decomposers respire as they break down the log, which releases CO<sub>2</sub> into the air.
check.hint: Only two processes on the list take CO<sub>2</sub> out of the air.
check.explain:
Removes: photosynthesis (plants use CO2 to make sugar) and the ocean absorbing CO2.

Adds: respiration, burning gasoline, decomposition, and volcanoes.

Decomposition sounds like "removing," but decomposers release the log's carbon as CO2.

screens.title: Carbon cycle data
screens.html:
On the GED, the carbon cycle usually appears as a graph of CO2 over time. Match the direction of change to a process:

  • CO2 falling needs a process that removes it, usually photosynthesis.
  • CO2 rising needs a process that adds it: respiration, decomposition, or burning.

Tell a seasonal pattern from a long-term trend. Each year CO2 falls during the Northern Hemisphere growing season and rises in fall and winter. Over decades, the yearly average has climbed, mainly because burning fossil fuels releases, in a short time, carbon that was stored for millions of years, and clearing forests leaves fewer trees to remove it.

example.prompt: Average atmospheric CO2 was about 316 ppm in 1959 and about 421 ppm in 2023 (yearly averages measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii). How much did it rise?
steps: Subtract: 421 − 316 = 105.
The rise is about 105 ppm, a long-term trend, not a seasonal swing.

check.prompt: Atmospheric CO2 rose from about 316 ppm in 1959 to about 421 ppm in 2023 (yearly averages measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii). Which statement best explains this long-term rise?
options: Burning fossil fuels releases stored carbon faster than photosynthesis and oceans can remove it.
Increased photosynthesis by forests and ocean algae has added more CO<sub>2</sub> to the air.
Trees lose their leaves each fall, so photosynthesis slows and CO<sub>2</sub> builds up every year.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in farm soils give off CO<sub>2</sub> as they turn nitrogen into ammonia.
why: Photosynthesis removes CO<sub>2</sub> from the air; it cannot be the cause of a rise.
Leaf loss explains the seasonal rise each winter, but CO<sub>2</sub> falls again every spring and summer. A seasonal cycle cannot explain a climb that lasts for decades.
Nitrogen fixation is part of the nitrogen cycle; it turns nitrogen gas into ammonia and is not a main source of CO<sub>2</sub>.
check.hint: Which process adds CO<sub>2</sub> and has grown steadily for decades?
check.explain: A decades-long rise needs a source that adds more CO2 than is removed, year after year. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon stored for millions of years faster than photosynthesis and oceans take it back. The leaf-loss choice is tempting, but it describes a seasonal swing that reverses every year.

screens.title: The nitrogen cycle
screens.html:
Air is about 78% nitrogen gas (N2), and living things need nitrogen to build proteins and DNA. But plants and animals cannot use nitrogen gas directly. Bacteria do most of the work:

  1. Nitrogen fixation: bacteria in soil and in the root nodules of beans, peas, and clover change N2 into ammonia. Lightning also fixes a small amount of nitrogen.
  2. Nitrification: other soil bacteria change ammonia into nitrates.
  3. Assimilation: plants absorb nitrates through their roots and build proteins. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
  4. Ammonification: decomposers return nitrogen from dead things and wastes to the soil as ammonia.
  5. Denitrification: bacteria, often in waterlogged soil, change nitrates back into N2, which returns to the air.

Farmers rotate crops, planting beans one year and corn the next, because the bean plants' root bacteria leave usable nitrogen in the soil.

check.prompt: Read the description of nitrogen in a garden. Click the sentence that describes nitrification.
spans: Lightning during a summer storm changes a little nitrogen gas into a form plants can use.
Bacteria in the bumps on the pea plants' roots change nitrogen gas into ammonia.
Other bacteria in the soil change that ammonia into nitrates.
The tomato plants take up nitrates through their roots and use the nitrogen to make proteins.
When the old plants rot, decomposers release ammonia back into the soil.
In a soggy corner of the garden, bacteria turn nitrates into nitrogen gas that escapes to the air.
check.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about bacteria in the pea roots. That is nitrogen fixation: it starts with nitrogen gas. Nitrification starts with ammonia and ends with nitrates.
check.explain:
Nitrification is the step in which soil bacteria change ammonia into nitrates: "Other bacteria in the soil change that ammonia into nitrates."

The lightning and pea-root sentences describe fixation (nitrogen gas into usable forms). The tomato sentence is assimilation, the rotting plants sentence is ammonification, and the soggy corner sentence is denitrification.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Natural selection: Variation, Inheritance, Overproduction, Selection (Very Interesting Organisms Survive). Populations evolve; acquired traits are not inherited; the trait must exist first.
  • Evidence: fossils, homologous structures (same bones), vestigial structures, embryos, DNA and proteins. Fewer differences = more recent common ancestor. Analogous structures (same job, different build) do not show close relationship.
  • Food chains: arrows point toward the eater. Producer → primary → secondary → tertiary. Decomposers recycle every level. Remove a predator: prey ↑, prey's food ↓.
  • Energy: about 10% passes up each level. Up: × 0.10. Down: × 10. Count arrows. Actual % = higher ÷ lower × 100.
  • Cycles: energy flows; matter cycles. Photosynthesis and oceans remove CO2; respiration, decomposition, burning, and volcanoes add it. Bacteria fix nitrogen, convert it to nitrates, and return it to the air.

Routine for every question: check the direction first: the trend, the arrow, or adding versus removing.

Next, go to Practice and start with Set A.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the trend in the lizard population from 2010 to 2020?
options: The number of dark lizards increased while the number of light lizards decreased.
The numbers of both light and dark lizards increased.
The number of light lizards increased while the number of dark lizards decreased.
The total number of lizards dropped to about half of its 2010 size.
why: Light lizards fell from 480 to 150, so both did not increase. Read each color's column from top to bottom on its own.
You reversed the two columns. Light lizards went from 480 down to 150, while dark lizards went from 120 up to 450.
The total stayed between 560 and 600 and was 600 in both 2010 and 2020. Only the mix of colors changed, not the size of the population.
items.hint: Read each column from top to bottom. Which column goes up, and which goes down?
items.explain:
Dark lizards went from 120 (2010) to 450 (2020), an increase. Light lizards went from 480 to 150, a decrease. So dark increased while light decreased.

The reversed statement (light increased, dark decreased) is the most common error from reading the columns in the wrong order. The total did not drop by half: it stayed between 560 and 600 the whole time and was 600 in both 2010 and 2020.

items.prompt: Based on the food web, which organism is only a primary consumer?
options: Rabbit
Grass
Frog
Snake
why: Grass is the producer. It makes its own food by photosynthesis and eats nothing, so it is not a consumer at all.
The frog eats grasshoppers, which are primary consumers, so the frog is a secondary consumer.
The snake eats mice and frogs, which are consumers, so the snake is a secondary or tertiary consumer, not a primary one.
items.hint: A primary consumer eats producers. Find an animal whose only food is a producer.
items.explain:
A primary consumer eats producers. The rabbit eats only grass, which is a producer, so the rabbit is a primary consumer.

Grass is a producer, not a consumer. The frog eats grasshoppers (primary consumers), so the frog is a secondary consumer. The snake eats mice and frogs, so it is a secondary or tertiary consumer, depending on the chain.

items.prompt: Each statement describes one condition of natural selection in the lizard population. Drag each statement to the condition it describes.
choices: Some lizards in the population are light tan and some are dark brown.
Dark parents usually have dark offspring.
Each female lays more eggs than can possibly survive to adulthood.
On the dark rock, hawks catch more light lizards than dark lizards.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the hawk statement under Variation. That statement is not about how lizards differ; it is about which lizards survive, which is selection.
items.hint: Variation = differences. Inheritance = passed to offspring. Overproduction = too many young. Selection = some survive better than others.
items.explain:
• Variation: lizards differ in color (light tan or dark brown).
  • Inheritance: color passes from parents to offspring.
  • Overproduction: more eggs are laid than can survive, so not every lizard can make it.
  • Selection: on dark rock, light lizards are easier for predators to see, so dark lizards survive and reproduce more.

A common mix-up is putting the predator statement under Variation. The predator statement is not about differences between lizards; it is about which lizards survive, which is selection.

items.prompt: What percentage of the lizards counted in 2020 were dark?

mistakes.why: You divided dark lizards by light lizards (450 ÷ 150 = 3). A percent of the population divides by the total for that year: 450 ÷ 600.
25% is the share of light lizards in 2020 (150 ÷ 600). The question asks for dark lizards: 450 ÷ 600.
0.75 is the decimal. Multiply by 100 to write it as a percent: 75.

items.hint: Divide the number of dark lizards in 2020 by the total for 2020, then multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Dark lizards in 2020 = 450. Total in 2020 = 600.

450 ÷ 600 = 0.75

0.75 × 100 = 75%

A common error is dividing by the number of light lizards (450 ÷ 150 = 3, or 300%). The percentage of a population always uses the total as the denominator. For comparison, dark lizards were 120 ÷ 600 = 20% of the population in 2010.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the change in the lizard population between 2010 and 2020?
options: Dark lizards were harder for hawks and gulls to spot on the dark rock, so more of them survived and passed dark coloring to their young.
Light lizards gradually changed to a dark color during their lives so that they would blend in better with the new dark rock.
Chemicals from the lava caused mutations that turned light lizards dark in response to the new environment.
The total population grew rapidly after the lava flow, so there was enough food for more dark lizards to survive.
why: Individual lizards cannot change their inherited color during their lives. That would be an acquired change, and the passage says color is inherited.
The environment does not create mutations on demand. Dark lizards (120 of them) already existed in 2010, before the lava flow could have any effect.
The total did not grow rapidly; it stayed between 560 and 600. More food also would not explain why one color increased and the other decreased.
items.hint: Use the four conditions. Which lizards were more likely to survive long enough to have offspring?
items.explain:
This is natural selection. Dark coloring already existed (variation) and is inherited. On dark rock, predators that hunt by sight spotted light lizards more easily, so dark lizards survived and reproduced more. Over several generations (each lizard lives only 2 to 3 years), dark lizards became a larger share of the population.

The idea that light lizards changed color during their lives describes an acquired change in individuals; individuals do not evolve, and the passage says color is inherited. Mutations are random and are not produced on demand by the environment; the dark lizards were present before the lava flow. The population did not grow rapidly; the total stayed between 560 and 600.

One food chain in this web is: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk.

In this chain, the frog is a {{0}}. The arrows point toward the organism that {{1}}. The fungi and bacteria in the web are {{2}}.

The grasshopper is the primary consumer because it eats the grass. The frog eats the grasshopper, one level higher.
The snake is the tertiary consumer. Count the consumers: grasshopper first, frog second.

options: receives the energy
