Only producers make their own food, and arrows point to eaters at every level, including animals.

options: producers
decomposers
primary consumers
why: Producers make food from sunlight. Fungi and bacteria get their energy from dead matter and wastes.
Primary consumers eat living producers. Organisms that break down dead remains are decomposers.

items.hint: Count the steps: grass is the producer, and the grasshopper eats the grass. Read each arrow as “is eaten by.”
items.explain:
Blank 1: Grass is the producer, the grasshopper is the primary consumer, and the frog, which eats the grasshopper, is the secondary consumer.

Blank 2: Arrows show the direction energy flows, from the food to the eater, so they point to the organism that receives the energy. Choosing “is eaten” reverses the arrow.

Blank 3: Fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms and wastes, so they are decomposers.

items.prompt: A disease kills most of the frogs in this grassland. Which change would most likely happen first?
options: The grasshopper population would increase, because fewer frogs would be eating grasshoppers.
The grass population would increase, because more grasshoppers would survive.
The snake population would increase, because snakes would have less competition for food.
The mouse population would decrease, because mice depend on frogs for food.
why: More grasshoppers would eat more grass, so grass would likely decrease. This choice reverses the second step.
Snakes eat frogs, so losing frogs takes away part of the snakes' food. Snakes would not increase.
Mice eat grass seeds and grasshoppers, not frogs, so the reason given is false.
items.hint: Find what the frog eats. If its predator disappears, what happens to that prey?
items.explain:
According to the table, frogs eat grasshoppers. With most frogs gone, fewer grasshoppers are eaten, so the grasshopper population would most likely increase. This is the most direct, first effect.

The grass would not increase; more grasshoppers would eat more grass, so grass would likely decrease. Snakes eat frogs, so losing frogs takes away part of the snakes' food; snakes would not increase. Mice do not eat frogs (they eat grass seeds and grasshoppers), so the reason given for the mouse choice is false.

items.prompt: Read the description of the nitrogen cycle. Click the sentence that describes nitrogen fixation.
spans: Nitrogen gas makes up about 78 percent of the air, but most living things cannot use nitrogen in this form.
Bacteria living in small bumps on the roots of bean and clover plants change nitrogen gas into ammonia.
Other soil bacteria change ammonia into nitrates.
Plants absorb nitrates through their roots and use the nitrogen to build proteins.
When plants and animals die, decomposers break down their remains and release ammonia into the soil.
Bacteria in waterlogged soil change nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the last sentence, about nitrates changing back into nitrogen gas. That is denitrification, the reverse of fixation. Fixation starts with nitrogen gas and makes ammonia.
items.hint: Nitrogen fixation turns nitrogen gas from the air into a form living things can use.
items.explain:
Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of nitrogen gas (N2) into a usable form such as ammonia. The sentence about bacteria in bean and clover root bumps (nodules) changing nitrogen gas into ammonia describes exactly that.

The other sentences describe other steps: ammonia to nitrates is nitrification; plants absorbing nitrates is assimilation; decomposers releasing ammonia is ammonification; and nitrates changing back to nitrogen gas is denitrification, the reverse of fixation. The first sentence gives background but describes no process.

items.prompt: The producers in a meadow capture 30,000 kcal of energy per square meter per year. Using the 10% rule, how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?

mistakes.why: 3,000 kcal is the primary consumer level. Secondary consumers are one more step up: 3,000 × 0.10 = 300.
You subtracted 10% instead of keeping 10% (30,000 − 3,000 = 27,000, then 27,000 − 2,700 = 24,300). The rule says only about 10% is passed on, so multiply by 0.10 each time.
30 kcal takes three steps, which is the tertiary level. Producers to secondary consumers is only two steps.

items.hint: Go up two levels: producers to primary consumers, then primary to secondary. Multiply by 0.10 each time.
items.explain:
Producers: 30,000 kcal

Primary consumers: 30,000 × 0.10 = 3,000 kcal

Secondary consumers: 3,000 × 0.10 = 300 kcal

A common error is stopping after one step (3,000 kcal), which is the energy for primary consumers. Another is subtracting 10% at each step (30,000 − 3,000 = 27,000, then 27,000 − 2,700 = 24,300). The rule says only about 10% is passed on.

items.prompt: Which two pairs are homologous structures, the kind of evidence that suggests the two animals share a common ancestor? Select two answers.
options: A horse's front leg and a mole's digging forelimb, which contain the same bones in the same order
A penguin's flipper and a sparrow's wing, which contain the same bones in the same order
A dragonfly's wing and a hummingbird's wing, which are both used for hovering in the air
An octopus eye and a human eye, which both focus light but form in different ways
A cactus's spines and a porcupine's quills, which both protect against animals that eat them
why: These do the same job, but a dragonfly wing has no bones. Same job with a different build makes them analogous, not homologous.
Both eyes focus light, but they develop in different ways from different tissues. That makes them analogous structures.
Spines and quills do the same job, but one is part of a plant and the other is hair on a mammal. They are analogous.
items.hint: Homologous means the same build (the same bones), even if the jobs are different.
items.explain:
Homologous structures have the same underlying structure, even when they do different jobs. A horse leg (running) and a mole forelimb (digging) share the same bones, and so do a penguin flipper (swimming) and a sparrow wing (flying). That shared build suggests a common ancestor.

The other pairs do the same job with different builds, which makes them analogous. The dragonfly and hummingbird wings are the most tempting, because both hover, but a dragonfly wing has no bones at all.

items.prompt: Between which two trophic levels was the percentage of energy transferred the greatest?
options: From primary consumers to secondary consumers
From producers to primary consumers
From secondary consumers to tertiary consumers
The percentage was exactly 10% between every pair of levels.
why: This step moved the most kilocalories (1,200), but as a percent it was only 1,200 ÷ 15,000 = 8%. The question asks for percentage, not amount.
12 ÷ 150 = 0.08, or 8%. That is lower than the 12.5% from primary to secondary consumers.
The 10% rule is an estimate. Dividing the measured values gives 8%, 12.5%, and 8%, so the transfers were not all exactly 10%.
items.hint: For each step, divide the higher level's energy by the level below it and multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Calculate each transfer percentage:

Producers → primary: 1,200 ÷ 15,000 = 0.08 = 8%

Primary → secondary: 150 ÷ 1,200 = 0.125 = 12.5%

Secondary → tertiary: 12 ÷ 150 = 0.08 = 8%

The greatest percentage, 12.5%, is from primary consumers to secondary consumers.

The producers-to-primary step moved the greatest amount of energy (1,200 kcal), but the question asks for the greatest percentage, and that step was only 8%. The 10% rule is an approximation; real measurements vary, as these data show.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the CO2 level falls from May to September?
options: Plants in the Northern Hemisphere are growing and remove large amounts of CO<sub>2</sub> from the air through photosynthesis.
People burn more fossil fuels to run air conditioners in the summer months, and burning those fuels removes CO<sub>2</sub> from the air.
Animals stop cellular respiration during the warm months, so they release no CO<sub>2</sub>.
Decomposers break down more dead leaves in summer, which takes CO<sub>2</sub> out of the air.
why: Burning fossil fuels adds CO2 to the air; it does not remove it. This choice reverses the direction of the process.
Animals carry out cellular respiration every moment they are alive, in every season. Respiration never stops.
Decomposition releases CO2 as decomposers respire. It adds carbon to the air; it does not take it out.
items.hint: Which carbon cycle process removes CO<sub>2</sub> from the air, and when is it strongest in the Northern Hemisphere?
items.explain:
From May to September, the level drops from 424.0 ppm to 418.0 ppm, a decrease of 424.0 − 418.0 = 6.0 ppm. This is the Northern Hemisphere growing season. Leafy plants carry out a great deal of photosynthesis, which takes CO2 out of the air faster than respiration and other processes put it back. In fall and winter, photosynthesis slows while respiration and decomposition continue, so CO2 rises again.

Burning fossil fuels adds CO2; it does not remove it. Animals never stop cellular respiration while alive. Decomposition releases CO2 to the air; it does not remove it.

items.prompt:
Scientists compared the amino acid sequence of one protein in humans with the same protein in five other animals. The table shows the number of amino acid differences from the human version. (Values are for a classroom example.)

AnimalDifferences from human protein
Chimpanzee1
Mouse9

Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
options: Humans and mice share a more recent common ancestor than humans and frogs do.
Humans evolved directly from chimpanzees.
Of the animals listed, fish are the most closely related to humans.
Chickens and frogs are more closely related to each other than either is to humans.
why: Only 1 difference shows a very recent common ancestor, not that humans came from today's chimpanzees. Both species descended from an earlier ancestor.
You reversed the rule. Fish have the most differences (24), so they are the least closely related on the list.
The table compares each animal only with humans. It gives no information about how chickens and frogs compare with each other.
items.hint: Fewer differences in a protein means two species are more closely related, sharing a more recent common ancestor.
items.explain:
Fewer amino acid differences indicate a closer relationship. The mouse protein has 9 differences from the human protein and the frog protein has 19. Since 9 < 19, humans are more closely related to mice, so humans and mice share a more recent common ancestor than humans and frogs do.

Only 1 difference with chimpanzees shows a very recent common ancestor, not that humans came from today's chimpanzees; both species descended from an earlier ancestor. Fish have the most differences (24), so they are the least closely related on the list. The table compares each animal only with humans, so it gives no information about how chickens and frogs compare with each other.

items.prompt: In a grassland, one food chain is grass → grasshopper → shrew → owl. The owls need about 45 kcal per square meter per year. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy must the grass capture to support them?
options: 45,000 kcal
4,500 kcal
0.045 kcal
why: 4,500 kcal is the grasshopper level (45 × 10 = 450 for shrews, 450 × 10 = 4,500). You stopped one step before the grass.
You multiplied by 10 four times, once for each organism. There are only three arrows between grass and owl, so multiply by 10 three times.
You multiplied by 0.10, which moves up the pyramid. To find the producers' energy, go down: multiply by 10 for each arrow.
items.hint: Go down the pyramid one arrow at a time, multiplying by 10 each time. Count the arrows.
items.explain:
Going down the pyramid, multiply by 10 for each arrow:

Shrews: 45 × 10 = 450 kcal

Grasshoppers: 450 × 10 = 4,500 kcal

Grass: 4,500 × 10 = 45,000 kcal

Check: three arrows means × 1,000 in all, and 45 × 1,000 = 45,000. Multiplying four times (450,000) counts organisms instead of arrows.

items.prompt:
Arctic permafrost is soil that has stayed frozen for thousands of years. It holds the remains of plants that died long ago and never decayed. Scientists warmed small plots of permafrost soil and measured the carbon dioxide (CO2) released. (Illustrative data.)

Soil temperature (°C)−50510
CO2 released (grams per square meter per day)0.10.41.83.6

Which statement best explains the pattern in the data?
options: As the soil thaws, decomposers break down the old plant remains, and their respiration releases the stored carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>.
Warmer soil lets the old plant remains carry out photosynthesis again, and photosynthesis gives off CO<sub>2</sub> into the air.
Frozen soil releases more CO<sub>2</sub> than thawed soil, because decomposers in the permafrost work fastest when it is cold.
Melting ice in the soil releases nitrogen gas, and soil bacteria change that nitrogen gas into CO<sub>2</sub> as it warms.
why: The plants died long ago and cannot photosynthesize. Also, photosynthesis removes CO<sub>2</sub> from the air; it does not release it.
This reverses the data. CO<sub>2</sub> released rose from 0.1 at −5 °C to 3.6 at 10 °C, so warmer soil released more, not less.
This mixes up the nitrogen and carbon cycles. Bacteria do not turn nitrogen gas into CO<sub>2</sub>; the carbon comes from the stored plant remains.
items.hint: Which carbon-cycle process releases CO<sub>2</sub> from dead plant matter, and does it speed up or slow down when it is warmer?
items.explain:
The CO2 released rises with temperature: 0.1 → 0.4 → 1.8 → 3.6 grams per square meter per day. Permafrost stores carbon in plant remains that decomposers could not break down while frozen. As the soil warms, decomposers become active, break down the remains, and release the carbon as CO2 through respiration.

The photosynthesis choice is the most tempting wrong answer, but photosynthesis removes CO2 and dead plants cannot do it. The cold-soil choice reads the data backward.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the trend in the male guppy population from 2012 to 2022?
options: The number of dull males increased while the number of bright males decreased.
The number of bright males increased while the number of dull males decreased.
The numbers of both bright males and dull males decreased every two years.
The total number of male guppies dropped to less than half of its 2012 size.
why: You reversed the two columns. Bright males fell from 360 to 80, while dull males rose from 140 to 320.
Dull males rose every two years, from 140 to 320, so both groups did not decrease. Read each column on its own.
The total fell from 500 to 400, which is 80% of the 2012 size, not less than half. Half of 500 would be 250.
items.hint: Read the bright column from top to bottom, then the dull column. Which goes up and which goes down?
items.explain:
Dull males went from 140 (2012) to 320 (2022), an increase. Bright males went from 360 to 80, a decrease. So dull males increased while bright males decreased.

The reversed statement comes from mixing up the columns. The total did fall, but only from 500 to 400 (400 ÷ 500 = 0.8, or 80% of the starting size), not to less than half.

items.prompt: Based on the pond food web, which organism is only a primary consumer?
options: Tadpole
Duckweed
Dragonfly nymph
Heron
why: Duckweed makes its own food by photosynthesis, so it is a producer, not a consumer.
Dragonfly nymphs eat mosquito larvae and tadpoles, which are primary consumers, so the nymph is a secondary consumer.
Herons eat sunfish and tadpoles, which are consumers, so the heron is a higher-level consumer, never a primary one.
items.hint: A primary consumer eats producers. Find an animal whose only foods are producers.
items.explain:
Tadpoles eat algae and duckweed. Both are producers, so the tadpole is only a primary consumer.

Duckweed is a producer. The dragonfly nymph eats other consumers, so it is a secondary consumer, and the heron eats sunfish and tadpoles, so it is at a higher level still.

items.prompt: Each statement describes one condition of natural selection in the guppy population. Drag each statement to the condition it describes.
choices: Some male guppies have large bright spots, and others have small faint spots.
Sons usually have color patterns like their fathers'.
Each female gives birth to far more young than can survive in the stream.
The new predator catches more bright males than dull males.
items.why: The most common mix-up is putting the predator statement under Overproduction because it is about guppies dying. It names which guppies die more often because of a trait, and that is selection.
items.hint: Variation = differences. Inheritance = passed to offspring. Overproduction = too many young. Selection = some survive better than others because of a trait.
items.explain:
• Variation: males differ in color pattern.
  • Inheritance: sons get color patterns like their fathers'.
  • Overproduction: more young are born than can survive.
  • Selection: the predator catches more bright males, so dull males survive and reproduce more.

The predator statement belongs under Selection, not Overproduction: it describes which guppies die, based on their color.

items.prompt: What percentage of the male guppies counted in 2022 were dull? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: You divided dull males by bright males (320 ÷ 80 = 4). A percent of the population divides by the total: 320 ÷ 400.
20% is the share of bright males in 2022 (80 ÷ 400). The question asks for dull males.
28% is the share of dull males in 2012 (140 ÷ 500). Use the 2022 row.

items.hint: Divide the number of dull males in 2022 by the total for 2022, then multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Dull males in 2022 = 320. Total in 2022 = 400.

320 ÷ 400 = 0.8

0.8 × 100 = 80%

Dividing by the bright males instead of the total (320 ÷ 80 = 4, or 400%) is the most common error. For comparison, dull males were 140 ÷ 500 = 28% of the males in 2012.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the change in the guppy population between 2012 and 2022?
options: Bright males were easier for the predator to spot, so dull males survived more often and passed dull coloring to their sons.
Bright males faded to a dull color during their lives so that the new predator would be less likely to notice them.
The predator's presence caused mutations in the guppies, which turned many of the bright males into dull males.
The predator ate mostly the young guppies, so the adult population grew and more dull males were able to find food.
why: Individual guppies do not change their inherited color to hide. That would be an acquired change in individuals, and populations, not individuals, evolve.
The predator did not create the dull trait. Dull males (140 of them) already existed in 2012, and mutations are random, not produced on demand.
The adult population did not grow; the total fell from 500 to 400. More food would also not explain why one color rose while the other fell.
items.hint: Use the four conditions. Which males were more likely to survive long enough to father young?
items.explain:
This is natural selection. Dull coloring already existed (variation) and is inherited. The predator hunts by sight and spots bright males more easily, so dull males survived and reproduced more. Over several generations, dull males became the majority.

The idea that bright males faded during their lives describes an acquired change in individuals. The mutation choice wrongly says the environment created the trait; dull males were already present in 2012.

items.prompt:
One food chain in this web is: algae → mosquito larvae → dragonfly nymph → sunfish → heron.

In this chain, the sunfish is a {{0}}, and it is at {{1}}. The energy available to the herons is {{2}} the energy captured by the algae.

options: primary consumer
secondary consumer
tertiary consumer
producer
why: Mosquito larvae are the primary consumers because they eat the algae. The sunfish is two levels above them.
The dragonfly nymph is the secondary consumer. The sunfish eats the nymph, one level higher.
Producers make their own food. The sunfish eats dragonfly nymphs, so it is a consumer.

options: trophic level 2
trophic level 3
trophic level 4
trophic level 5
why: Level 2 is the mosquito larvae. Count the algae as level 1: algae 1, larvae 2, nymph 3, sunfish 4.
Level 3 is the dragonfly nymph. You may have counted consumers only; trophic levels start at 1 with the producer.
Level 5 is the heron, the last organism in the chain.

options: much less than
about equal to
greater than
why: Only about 10% passes up each level, so after four steps the herons have roughly 0.01% of the algae's energy, not an equal amount.
Energy decreases at each level because most is used and lost as heat. A top consumer can never have more energy than the producers.

items.hint: Count the algae as trophic level 1. Remember how much energy passes up each level.
items.explain:
Blank 1: Algae are producers, mosquito larvae are primary consumers, dragonfly nymphs are secondary consumers, and the sunfish is the tertiary consumer.

Blank 2: Counting algae as level 1, the sunfish is at trophic level 4.

Blank 3: About 10% passes up each level, so the heron's level, four steps up, has much less energy than the algae (about 0.10 × 0.10 × 0.10 × 0.10 = 0.0001 of it).

items.prompt: A disease kills most of the dragonfly nymphs in the pond. Which change would most likely happen first?
options: The mosquito larvae population would increase, because fewer dragonfly nymphs would be eating them.
The algae population would increase, because more mosquito larvae would survive to eat them.
The sunfish population would increase, because sunfish would have fewer nymphs to compete with.
The heron population would decrease right away, because herons depend on dragonfly nymphs for their food.
why: More mosquito larvae would eat more algae, so algae would likely decrease. This choice reverses the second step.
Sunfish eat dragonfly nymphs; they do not compete with them. Losing the nymphs takes away the sunfish's only food, so sunfish would decrease.
Herons eat sunfish and tadpoles, not dragonfly nymphs, so the reason given is false.
items.hint: Find what the dragonfly nymphs eat. If their predator disappears, what happens to that prey?
items.explain:
Dragonfly nymphs eat mosquito larvae and tadpoles. With most nymphs gone, fewer larvae are eaten, so the mosquito larvae population would most likely increase. This is the most direct, first effect.

The algae would not increase; more larvae would eat more algae. Sunfish eat only dragonfly nymphs, so they would lose their food and decrease. Herons do not eat nymphs, so the heron choice rests on a false reason.

items.prompt: Read the description of nitrogen on a farm. Click the sentence that describes the step that returns nitrogen gas to the air.
spans: Clover growing in the pasture has root nodules full of bacteria that turn nitrogen gas into ammonia.
Soil bacteria change the ammonia into nitrates.
The farmer's corn absorbs nitrates through its roots and uses the nitrogen to build proteins.
Cows eat the corn, and their manure adds nitrogen to the soil.
Decomposers break down the manure and release ammonia.
After heavy rains flood the low field, bacteria in the soggy soil change nitrates into nitrogen gas.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the clover sentence, because it also mentions nitrogen gas. In that sentence nitrogen gas is being taken out of the air (fixation); the soggy-soil sentence describes denitrification, which sends it back.
items.hint: Look for the step that ends with nitrogen gas, not the step that starts with it.
items.explain:
Denitrification returns nitrogen to the air: bacteria change nitrates back into nitrogen gas, often in waterlogged soil. That is the sentence about bacteria in the soggy soil after the flood.

The clover sentence describes fixation, the opposite step. The other sentences describe nitrification (ammonia to nitrates), assimilation (corn absorbing nitrates), animals passing nitrogen on in wastes, and ammonification (decomposers releasing ammonia).

items.prompt: In a salt marsh, the cordgrass captures 45,000 kcal of energy per square meter per year. One food chain is cordgrass → grasshopper → spider → wren. Using the 10% rule, how much energy is available to the wrens? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 450 kcal is the spider level. The wrens are one more step up: 450 × 0.10 = 45.
You took four steps, one for each organism. There are only three arrows from cordgrass to wren, so multiply by 0.10 three times.
You subtracted 10% at each step (45,000 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9). Only about 10% is passed on, so multiply by 0.10.

items.hint: Count the arrows from the cordgrass to the wren. Multiply by 0.10 once for each arrow.
items.explain:
Grasshoppers: 45,000 × 0.10 = 4,500 kcal

Spiders: 4,500 × 0.10 = 450 kcal

Wrens: 450 × 0.10 = 45 kcal

Three arrows means the wrens get 0.10 × 0.10 × 0.10 = 0.001 of the producers' energy. Stopping a step early (450) or taking an extra step (4.5) are the most common errors.

items.prompt: Which two observations are examples of vestigial structures? Select two answers.
options: Some whales have small hip bones inside their bodies that are not attached to any legs.
Some blind fish that live in dark caves have small eyes covered over by skin.
A bat's wing and a human's arm contain the same bones arranged in the same order.
Early embryos of fish, chickens, and humans all have tails and pouches in the neck.
Two bird species differ at only 3 bases in a gene that is 1,000 bases long.
why: Same bones used for different jobs are homologous structures. Both the wing and the arm are fully used, so neither is vestigial.
This is evidence from embryos (comparative embryology), not a reduced body part in an adult.
This is DNA evidence. Few differences suggest a recent common ancestor, but no body part is being described.
items.hint: A vestigial structure is a reduced part that has little or no use now but was useful to the ancestors.
items.explain:
Vestigial structures are reduced parts with little or no use today. Whale hip bones attached to no legs, and skin-covered eyes in blind cave fish, both fit: the ancestors of these animals used legs and sight.

The bat wing and human arm are homologous structures, the tails and neck pouches are evidence from embryos, and the gene comparison is DNA evidence. All support evolution, but none is vestigial.

items.prompt: Between which two trophic levels was the percentage of energy transferred the lowest?
options: From producers to primary consumers
From secondary consumers to tertiary consumers
From primary consumers to secondary consumers
The percentage was exactly 10% between every pair of levels.
why: This step moved the smallest amount (18 kcal), but as a percent it was 18 ÷ 180 = 10%, which is higher than 5%.
180 ÷ 1,500 = 0.12, or 12%. That is the highest percentage in the table, not the lowest.
The 10% rule is only an estimate. The measured transfers were 5%, 12%, and 10%, so they were not all the same.
items.hint: For each step, divide the higher level's energy by the level below it and multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Calculate each transfer percentage:

Producers → primary: 1,500 ÷ 30,000 = 0.05 = 5%

Primary → secondary: 180 ÷ 1,500 = 0.12 = 12%

Secondary → tertiary: 18 ÷ 180 = 0.10 = 10%

The lowest percentage, 5%, is from producers to primary consumers, even though that step moved the most kilocalories. The secondary-to-tertiary step is tempting because it moved the smallest amount, but the question asks about percentage.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why CO2 decreased in Jar 1 but increased in Jar 2?
options: In light, the plant removed more CO<sub>2</sub> by photosynthesis than it released by respiration; in the dark it could only respire.
The plant carried out respiration only in the light and photosynthesis only in the dark, so the two jars changed in opposite ways.
The plant stopped all of its life processes in the dark, so CO<sub>2</sub> from the room air leaked into Jar 2 instead of being used.
Light made the pond water absorb CO<sub>2</sub> by itself, so Jar 1 lost CO<sub>2</sub> while the water in dark Jar 2 could not do so.
why: This reverses the two processes. Photosynthesis needs light; respiration happens in light and dark alike.
The jars were sealed, so no room air could leak in. A living plant keeps carrying out respiration in the dark, and that released the CO<sub>2</sub>.
Jar 5 held only pond water in the light, and its CO<sub>2</sub> did not change at all. Light alone does not make the water take in CO<sub>2</sub>.
items.hint: Which process needs light? Which process happens in light and in dark? Use Jar 5 to check the water itself.
items.explain:
Jar 1 (plant, light) fell by 150 ppm. In light, the plant does photosynthesis, which removes CO2, faster than its respiration adds CO2. Jar 2 (plant, dark) rose by 40 ppm: without light there is no photosynthesis, but the plant still carries out cellular respiration, which releases CO2.

Jar 5, the water-only control, shows the water itself caused no change, which rules out the water-absorbing choice. The snail in Jar 3 (+90) shows animals add CO2; in Jar 4, the plant's uptake outweighed the snail's release (−150 + 90 = −60).

items.prompt:
The table describes fossils found in four rock layers. Layer 1 is on top. (Simplified classroom example.)

LayerAgeFossil description
1 (top)About 40 million yearsFlippers; tiny hind legs not attached to the backbone; nostrils set farther back on the snout; lived only in water
2About 47 million yearsShort legs with wide, paddle-like feet; nostrils partway up the snout; lived mostly in water
3About 49 million yearsFour long legs; ear bones shaped like those of modern whales; lived on land near water
4 (bottom)About 52 million yearsFour-legged land mammal with ankle bones like those of hoofed mammals

Which conclusion is best supported by this fossil sequence?
options: Whales likely descended from land mammals through forms that lived more and more in the water.
Each animal's legs shrank during its life because it spent more of its time swimming in the water.
The land mammal in Layer 4 is proven to be the direct ancestor of every whale species alive today.
Whales evolved before land mammals did, because the fossils with flippers come first in the rock.
why: Fossils record changes across generations, not within one animal's life. A change from use or disuse is acquired and is not inherited.
Fossils can show a likely pattern of descent, but they cannot prove that one particular fossil animal is the direct ancestor of all whales.
You read the layers in the wrong order. Deeper layers are older, so the four-legged land mammal (Layer 4, 52 million years) came first.
items.hint: Deeper layers are older. Read the table from the bottom up and describe how the animals change.
items.explain:
Reading from the oldest layer (bottom) to the youngest (top): a land mammal, then a four-legged animal with whale-like ears that lived near water, then a mostly aquatic animal with short legs, then a fully aquatic animal with flippers and tiny unattached hind legs. These are transitional forms, so the best-supported conclusion is that whales likely descended from land mammals through forms that lived more and more in water.

The "whales came first" choice reverses the layer order. The "proven direct ancestor" choice overstates what fossils can show.

items.prompt: A person needs about 2,000 kcal of food energy a day. Suppose all of it comes from beef, through the chain corn → cattle → person. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy must the corn capture to supply the person for one day?
options: 20,000 kcal
200 kcal
why: 20,000 kcal is the cattle level (2,000 × 10). You stopped one step before the corn. That amount would supply the person only if the person ate the corn directly.
You multiplied by 10 three times, once for each organism. There are only two arrows from corn to person, so multiply by 10 twice.
You multiplied by 0.10, which moves up the pyramid. To find the producers' energy, go down: multiply by 10 for each arrow.
items.hint: The person is two arrows above the corn. Going down the pyramid, multiply by 10 for each arrow.
items.explain:
Going down the pyramid from the person:

Cattle: 2,000 × 10 = 20,000 kcal

Corn: 20,000 × 10 = 200,000 kcal

Compare: eating the corn directly would take only 2,000 × 10 = 20,000 kcal of corn energy, one tenth as much. Each extra level in a food chain multiplies the producer energy needed by about 10.

items.prompt:
Scientists measured carbon dioxide in the air and dissolved in surface seawater at one ocean station. Both are shown in the same units. (Simplified classroom values.)

Year1990200020102020
CO2 in the air354369389412
CO2 in surface seawater350366385408

Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: As CO<sub>2</sub> in the air rose, the ocean took in more of it, so the ocean is storing part of the added carbon.
The ocean is the main source of the added CO<sub>2</sub> in the air, because seawater levels rose during each decade too.
Ocean algae are doing less photosynthesis each decade, and that decline is the reason the CO<sub>2</sub> in the air rose.
Seawater cannot hold any more carbon, so the amount of CO<sub>2</sub> dissolved in the ocean will stop rising after 2020.
why: Rising together does not show which way carbon moves. Seawater stays a little below the air each year, which fits CO2 moving from the air into the water, not out of it.
The table has no data on algae or photosynthesis, so this explanation goes beyond the evidence.
Nothing in the data shows a limit. Seawater CO<sub>2</sub> rose in every decade, and by more each time (16, then 19, then 23), with no sign of leveling off.
items.hint: Which carbon-cycle process involves the ocean taking CO<sub>2</sub> from the air? Compare the two rows each year.
items.explain:
From 1990 to 2020, CO2 in the air rose 412 − 354 = 58 units, and CO2 in seawater rose 408 − 350 = 58 units. The seawater value tracks the air and stays slightly lower, which fits ocean water absorbing CO2 from the air, one of the two processes that remove CO2 from the atmosphere. So the ocean is storing part of the added carbon.

The "ocean is the source" choice is tempting because both rows rise, but rising together does not show the ocean releasing carbon. The algae and "cannot hold more" choices are not supported by these data.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the change in the bacteria population from Day 0 to Day 8?
options: A few bacteria already had the resistance gene; they survived the antibiotic and divided, so their share kept growing.
Each bacterium slowly got used to the antibiotic over several days, so most of them eventually stopped being harmed by it.
The antibiotic caused new resistance mutations in many bacteria, and those bacteria then passed the new gene to their offspring.
The total number of bacteria grew so large that there was plenty of food, which let the resistant bacteria survive better.
why: Individual bacteria do not "get used to" an antibiotic. Resistance comes from a gene; the population changed because resistant cells survived and divided.
The passage says resistant bacteria were present before the experiment began (0.5% on Day 0). The antibiotic selected the trait; it did not create it.
The data give the percent resistant, not the total number or the food supply. Plenty of food also would not explain why resistant cells did better.
items.explain:
This is natural selection. Variation: 0.5% of bacteria were resistant on Day 0. Inheritance: the gene is copied when a bacterium divides. Overproduction: bacteria divide many times a day. Selection: the antibiotic killed non-resistant cells, so resistant cells survived and divided, and their share rose to 93%.

The mutation choice is the most tempting, but the resistance gene was already there before any antibiotic was added.

directly created a brand-new
had no effect on the
why: Resistant bacteria were found before the experiment began, so the antibiotic did not create the trait; it let resistant cells survive while others died.
The share of resistant bacteria rose from 0.5% to 93% while the antibiotic was present, so it clearly affected which bacteria survived.
93% is the Day 8 value, not the change. Subtract the starting value: 93 − 0.5 = 92.5.

the antibiotic as the days went by

The antibiotic dose stayed the same every day. What changed was the bacteria population.

Blank 1: Resistant bacteria existed on Day 0, so the antibiotic favored an already existing trait; it did not create it.

Blank 2: 93 − 0.5 = 92.5 percentage points.

Blank 3: Evolution happens in the population over many generations, not in individuals. Bacteria divide many times a day, so eight days is many generations.

items.prompt: A mole's front limb, a horse's front leg, and a human arm contain the same set of bones in the same order. The mole uses its limb for digging, the horse for running, and the human for grasping. This observation is best described as which kind of evidence?
options: Homologous structures, which suggest the three animals share a common ancestor
Analogous structures, which show that animals with similar jobs develop similar bones
Vestigial structures, which show that these limbs no longer serve any purpose
Embryo evidence, which shows that the three animals look alike before they are born
why: Analogous structures do the same job with different builds. Here the jobs differ and the bones are the same, which is the opposite pattern.
Vestigial structures are reduced parts with little or no use. These limbs are fully used for digging, running, and grasping.
The observation is about the bones of adult limbs, not about how embryos look.
items.explain:
The same bones arranged the same way but used for different jobs are homologous structures. They suggest that moles, horses, and humans inherited the limb pattern from a common ancestor.

"Analogous" is the tempting wrong answer, but analogous structures share a job, not a build.

items.prompt: A disease kills most of the warblers in the forest. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Caterpillars would increase, and the oak trees could lose more of their leaves.
Snakes would increase, because they would face less competition from the warblers.
Chipmunks would decrease, because chipmunks depend on warblers as their food.
Deer would decrease, because the caterpillars would eat most of the grasses.
why: Snakes eat warblers; they do not compete with them. Losing warblers removes part of the snakes' food.
Chipmunks eat acorns and caterpillars, not warblers, so the reason given is false.
Caterpillars eat oak leaves, not grasses, so more caterpillars would not take the deer's grass.
items.explain:
Chain: oak leaves → caterpillars → warblers. With fewer warblers eating them, caterpillars increase, and more caterpillars eat more oak leaves, so oaks lose more leaves.

The snake choice is tempting, but snakes are predators of warblers, not competitors; they lose food when warblers die.

items.prompt: Use the producers' energy given above the table. In the food chain oak → caterpillar → warbler → black rat snake, how much energy is available to the snakes, according to the 10% rule? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 180 kcal is the warbler level. The snakes are one more step up: 180 × 0.10 = 18.
You took four steps, one for each organism. There are three arrows from oak to snake, so multiply by 0.10 three times.
You subtracted 10% at each step (18,000 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9). Only about 10% is passed on, so multiply by 0.10.

items.explain:
Caterpillars: 18,000 × 0.10 = 1,800 kcal

Warblers: 1,800 × 0.10 = 180 kcal

Snakes: 180 × 0.10 = 18 kcal

Three arrows means 18,000 ÷ 1,000 = 18. Stopping at 180 skips the last step.

items.prompt: In a different forest, scientists measured the energy stored in three levels: oak trees, 18,000 kcal; caterpillars, 1,440 kcal; warblers, 180 kcal (per square meter per year). Which statement about the transfer from caterpillars to warblers is supported?
options: About 12.5% was transferred, which is a little more than the 10% rule predicts.
About 8% was transferred, which is a little less than the 10% rule predicts.
About 1% was transferred, because 180 kcal is 1% of the oak trees' 18,000 kcal.
About 87.5% was transferred, because 1,440 − 180 = 1,260 kcal moved up.
why: 8% is the transfer from oak trees to caterpillars (1,440 ÷ 18,000). The question asks about caterpillars to warblers.
You compared the warblers with the producers, which skips a level. The transfer from caterpillars uses the caterpillars' energy: 180 ÷ 1,440.
1,260 kcal is the energy that did not reach the warblers. 1,260 ÷ 1,440 = 87.5% is the share lost, not the share transferred.
items.explain:
Actual % = higher level ÷ level below × 100.

180 ÷ 1,440 = 0.125

0.125 × 100 = 12.5%, a little more than the 10% estimate.

The 8% choice is tempting because it is a real transfer in the data, but it is the oak-to-caterpillar step.

items.prompt:
Two stations measure atmospheric CO2 for one year. (Simplified classroom values.)

StationLowest monthly value (ppm)Highest monthly value (ppm)
Northern Hemisphere (Hawaii)418.0424.0
Near the South Pole417.9419.0

Most of Earth's land, and most of its forests, are in the Northern Hemisphere. Which statement best explains why the seasonal swing is larger at the northern station?
options: More land plants up north means photosynthesis rises and falls more by season there.
No photosynthesis happens at all in the Southern Hemisphere, so CO<sub>2</sub> never changes.
Cold air at the South Pole stops cellular respiration, so CO<sub>2</sub> stays the same all year.
Plants in the Northern Hemisphere release CO<sub>2</sub> by photosynthesis during the summer.
why: The southern station still changes (from 417.9 to 419.0 ppm), and ocean algae and land plants in the south do carry out photosynthesis.
Respiration does not stop in the cold, and the southern station's CO<sub>2</sub> does change by about 1.1 ppm.
Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air. This choice reverses the direction of the process.
items.explain:
Northern swing: 424.0 − 418.0 = 6.0 ppm. Southern swing: 419.0 − 417.9 = 1.1 ppm. The Northern Hemisphere has far more land covered by leafy plants, so photosynthesis there removes much more CO2 in summer and much less in winter, creating a bigger seasonal swing.

The "no photosynthesis in the south" choice is contradicted by the data: the southern value still changes.

items.prompt: Which two processes produce nitrogen in a form that plants can absorb and use? Select two answers.
options: Bacteria in the root nodules of clover change nitrogen gas into ammonia.
Decomposers break down dead leaves and animal wastes and release ammonia.
Bacteria in waterlogged soil change nitrates into nitrogen gas.
Plant roots absorb nitrates from the soil to build proteins.
Plant leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air for photosynthesis.
why: This is denitrification. It turns usable nitrates into nitrogen gas, which plants cannot use, and sends it back to the air.
This is assimilation. Plants absorbing nitrates use nitrogen that is already in a usable form; this step does not produce any.
This is part of the carbon cycle. Taking in carbon dioxide produces no usable nitrogen.
items.explain:
Nitrogen fixation by root-nodule bacteria turns nitrogen gas into ammonia, and decomposers release ammonia from dead matter and wastes (ammonification). Both produce nitrogen in a form plants can use.

Denitrification is the tempting wrong answer because bacteria do it, but it turns usable nitrates back into nitrogen gas, taking usable nitrogen out of the soil. Plants absorbing nitrates uses nitrogen; it does not produce it.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the change in the pigweed population from Year 1 to Year 6?
options: A few plants already carried the resistance gene; they survived the spraying and their seeds grew into more resistant plants.
Pigweed plants exposed to the spray each spring slowly toughened over the years until most of them could survive it.
The weed killer caused new resistance mutations in many plants, and those plants then passed the new gene to their seeds.
The farmer sprayed less each year, so more of the pigweed plants survived and produced seeds that grew into new plants.
why: Individual plants do not toughen up and change their genes. The population changed because resistant plants survived and left more seeds.
The passage says resistant plants were present before the first spraying. The weed killer selected the trait; it did not create it.
The passage says the farmer sprayed the same weed killer every spring. Nothing says the amount went down.
items.explain:
This is natural selection. Variation: a few plants were resistant before spraying. Inheritance: resistant plants pass the gene to their seeds. Overproduction: each plant makes thousands of seeds. Selection: the spray killed most non-resistant plants, so resistant plants left more seeds, and their share rose from 1% to 90%.

The mutation choice is the most tempting, but the resistance gene existed before the weed killer was ever used.

was caused by the weed killer after it was sprayed
appeared because the plants needed it to survive
why: Scientists found resistant plants before the first spraying, so the weed killer did not cause the gene.
Genes do not appear because an organism needs them. Mutations are random; the spray only favored plants that already had the gene.
90% is the Year 6 value, not the change. Subtract the starting value: 90 − 1 = 89.

why: Each plant keeps the genes it was born with. Individuals do not evolve; the share of resistant plants in the population changed.
Nothing says the weed killer got weaker. The same product was used each year; the plants in the field changed.

items.explain:
Blank 1: The gene was present in a few plants before any spraying; the spray favored it but did not create it.

Blank 2: 90 − 1 = 89 percentage points.

Blank 3: What changed was the population, over several generations, not individual plants.

items.prompt: Early embryos of a fish, a chicken, and a human all have a tail and a series of pouches in the neck region, even though adult chickens and humans have no gills. This observation is best described as which kind of evidence?
options: Embryo evidence, which suggests these animals share a common ancestor
Fossil evidence, which shows the order in which these animals appeared
Analogous structures, which show that animals with the same jobs look alike
Vestigial structures, which are reduced adult parts that have no use today
why: Fossil evidence comes from preserved remains in rock layers. This observation comes from comparing living embryos.
Analogous structures do the same job with different builds. These embryos share the same build early on, which points to shared ancestry.
Vestigial structures are reduced parts in adults. The observation is about how early embryos look, before the tails and pouches change.
items.explain:
Similar features in early embryos, such as tails and neck pouches, are evidence that fish, chickens, and humans share a common ancestor. These features develop into different structures later, but the shared starting pattern was inherited.

"Vestigial structures" is tempting because the tail seems to disappear, but vestigial refers to reduced parts in adults, not to how embryos develop.

items.prompt: Hunters remove most of the sea otters from this coast. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Sea urchins would increase, and the kelp would decrease as more urchins graze on it.
Kelp would increase, because sea otters would no longer be eating so much of the kelp.
Small fish would increase, because sea otters would no longer be eating the small fish.
Harbor seals would decrease, because harbor seals depend on sea otters for their food.
why: Sea otters eat sea urchins and crabs, not kelp. Following the arrows, kelp would decrease, not increase.
Sea otters do not eat small fish. In fact, with more crabs surviving, small fish would likely decrease.
Harbor seals eat small fish and crabs, not sea otters, so the reason given is false.
items.explain:
Chain: kelp → sea urchin → sea otter. With fewer otters eating them, sea urchins increase, and more urchins eat more kelp, so kelp decreases.

The "kelp would increase" choice is the most tempting; it comes from skipping the urchins and assuming otters eat kelp. Move one arrow at a time.

items.prompt: Use the phytoplankton's energy given above the table. In the food chain phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → harbor seal, how much energy is available to the harbor seals, according to the 10% rule? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 400 kcal is the small fish level. The seals are one more step up: 400 × 0.10 = 40.
You took four steps, one for each organism. There are three arrows from phytoplankton to seal, so multiply by 0.10 three times.
You subtracted 10% at each step (40,000 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9). Only about 10% is passed on, so multiply by 0.10.

items.explain:
Zooplankton: 40,000 × 0.10 = 4,000 kcal

Small fish: 4,000 × 0.10 = 400 kcal

Harbor seals: 400 × 0.10 = 40 kcal

Three arrows means 40,000 ÷ 1,000 = 40. Stopping at 400 skips the last step.

items.prompt: In a different stretch of ocean, scientists measured the energy stored in three levels: phytoplankton, 40,000 kcal; zooplankton, 3,200 kcal; small fish, 288 kcal (per square meter per year). Which statement about the transfer from zooplankton to small fish is supported?
options: About 9% was transferred, which is a little less than the 10% rule predicts.
About 8% was transferred, which is a little less than the 10% rule predicts.
About 0.72% was transferred, because 288 kcal is 0.72% of the phytoplankton.
About 11% was transferred, because 3,200 ÷ 288 is a little more than 11.
why: 8% is the transfer from phytoplankton to zooplankton (3,200 ÷ 40,000). The question asks about zooplankton to small fish.
You compared the small fish with the producers, which skips a level. Use the zooplankton's energy: 288 ÷ 3,200.
You divided the lower level by the higher one. That gives a ratio of about 11, not a percent. Put the higher level on top: 288 ÷ 3,200.
items.explain:
Actual % = higher level ÷ level below × 100.

288 ÷ 3,200 = 0.09

0.09 × 100 = 9%, a little less than the 10% estimate.

The 8% choice is tempting because it is a real transfer in the data, but it is the phytoplankton-to-zooplankton step.

items.prompt: Coal, oil, and natural gas formed from organisms that took in carbon dioxide and lived millions of years ago. Which statement best explains why burning these fuels today raises the amount of CO2 in the air?
options: Burning releases, in a few years, carbon that was stored for millions of years, faster than plants and oceans remove it.
Burning these fuels removes oxygen from the air, and plants then release extra CO<sub>2</sub> to replace the missing oxygen.
The carbon in fossil fuels was never part of living things, so burning adds brand-new carbon that the cycle has never held.
Fossil fuels are made mostly of nitrogen, and burning changes the nitrogen in them into carbon dioxide gas in the air.
why: Plants do not release CO<sub>2</sub> to replace oxygen. Burning itself combines the fuel's carbon with oxygen to make CO<sub>2</sub>.
The prompt says fossil fuels formed from living things. Their carbon was once in the air; burning returns stored carbon, it does not create new carbon.
Fossil fuels are made mostly of carbon compounds, and burning cannot change one element into another.
items.explain:
The carbon in fossil fuels was removed from the air by ancient organisms and then stored underground for millions of years. Burning releases it as CO2 in a short time, faster than photosynthesis and the oceans can take it back, so the amount in the air rises.

The "brand-new carbon" choice is tempting, but the prompt itself says the fuels came from living things.

items.prompt: Which two steps of the nitrogen cycle are carried out by bacteria? Select two answers.
options: Changing nitrogen gas into ammonia in the root nodules of bean plants
Changing nitrates into nitrogen gas that returns to the air
Changing nitrogen gas into usable forms during a lightning strike
Absorbing nitrates through roots to build proteins
Getting nitrogen by eating plants or other animals
why: Lightning does fix some nitrogen, but it is a physical process, not something bacteria do.
Plants, not bacteria, absorb nitrates through their roots. This step is assimilation.
Animals get nitrogen by eating other organisms. No bacteria are involved in this step.
items.explain:
Bacteria carry out nitrogen fixation (in soil and in legume root nodules, turning nitrogen gas into ammonia) and denitrification (turning nitrates back into nitrogen gas). They also carry out nitrification.

Lightning is the tempting wrong choice because it also fixes nitrogen, but it is not done by bacteria. Plants absorb nitrates, and animals get nitrogen by eating.

vocab.def: A change in the inherited traits of a population over many generations.
vocab.example: Over 50 years, the average beak size in a bird population increased.

vocab.def: The process in which individuals with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common.
vocab.example: Dark lizards on dark rock are seen by birds less often, so more of them survive to have young.

vocab.def: An inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
vocab.example: A cactus's thick, waxy skin helps it hold water in the desert.

vocab.def: Differences in traits among individuals of the same species.
vocab.example: Some rabbits in a litter have thicker fur than others.

vocab.def: How well an organism survives and reproduces compared with others; measured by surviving offspring, not strength.
vocab.example: A small, well-hidden moth that has many offspring has high fitness.

vocab.def: An earlier species from which two or more later species are descended.
vocab.example: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor that lived millions of years ago.

vocab.def: Body parts in different species that have the same basic structure but may have different functions, suggesting a common ancestor.
vocab.example: A human arm, a bat wing, and a whale flipper have the same arrangement of bones.

vocab.def: A body part that is reduced and has little or no use in an organism today but was useful in its ancestors.
An organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis.
An organism that gets energy by eating other organisms; primary consumers eat producers, secondary consumers eat primary consumers, and so on.
vocab.example: A rabbit (primary) eating grass; a fox (secondary) eating the rabbit.

vocab.def: An organism that breaks down dead organisms and wastes and returns nutrients to the soil.
vocab.example: Mushrooms and bacteria breaking down a fallen log.

vocab.def: A diagram of many connected food chains in an ecosystem, with arrows pointing from the food to the eater.
vocab.example: A pond web linking algae, snails, insects, fish, frogs, and herons.

vocab.def: An organism's feeding position in a food chain, counted from the producers.
vocab.example: Grass is level 1; a grasshopper is level 2; a frog that eats the grasshopper is level 3.

vocab.def: A diagram showing that the energy available decreases at each higher trophic level; about 10% passes from one level to the next.
vocab.example: 10,000 kcal in plants → 1,000 kcal in rabbits → 100 kcal in foxes.

vocab.def: The changing of nitrogen gas from the air into a form living things can use, done mostly by bacteria.
vocab.example: Bacteria in the root bumps (nodules) of bean plants make ammonia from nitrogen gas.

notes:
Study Notes: Evolution and Ecosystems

Natural Selection: VIOS

Very Interesting Organisms Survive

  • Variation — individuals differ.
  • Inheritance — traits pass to offspring.
  • Overproduction — too many offspring; competition.
  • Selection — better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more.

Populations evolve, not individuals. Acquired traits are not inherited. The trait must exist before the change.

Evidence for Evolution

  • Fossils (older layers, transitional forms)
  • Homologous structures (same bones, different jobs)
  • Analogous structures (same job, different build) do not show close relationship
  • Vestigial structures (tailbone)
  • Similar embryos
  • DNA/protein: fewer differences = closer relatives

Food Chains and Webs

Producer → primary → secondary → tertiary consumer. Arrow points to the eater (energy flow). Decomposers recycle every level. Trophic levels count the producer as level 1.

10% Rule

Up one level: × 0.10. Down one level: × 10. Count the arrows, not the organisms.
Actual % = (higher level ÷ lower level) × 100.
90% is used for life processes and lost as heat, or is never eaten.

Cycles

Carbon: photosynthesis and oceans remove CO2; respiration, decomposition, burning, and volcanoes add CO2.
Nitrogen: fixation (N2 → ammonia, by bacteria; lightning fixes a little) → nitrification (→ nitrates) → plants absorb → decomposers return ammonia → denitrification (→ N2).
